I found that i flowed more smoothly for me because that is the type of content I gravitate toward. Excerpt 2 is more technically proficient in its delivery but it is arguably equal in quality because it is too familiar and said before, it loses the readers attention quickly.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick’s Day, though there was no room for festivity in the hospital room where my mother lay suspended between this life and the next. Outside, the sunlight refracted sharply off the icy snow, casting a dazzling brilliance that mocked the stillness inside. Beside her, a bowl of green Jell-O sat untouched, its lurid color out of place in the solemnity of the moment. My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room. She was there but not there—unresponsive, yet undeniably present. I watched her, saw her dying like a fire slowly extinguishing into smoke, the embers of her vitality winking out one by one. Her eyes, once fierce with bitterness, shifted to bewilderment, and finally, to a quiet, unspoken heroism. They were the eyes of someone who clung to life even as it slipped from her grasp, a desperate yearning embedded in that piercing blue. The blue of her eyes became my lodestar, a symbol of her fight, her grace, her inevitability. And as I held her hand, I knew that when she closed those eyes for the last time, they would remain etched in me forever, as luminous as the snow outside.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I just lost a friend, and what Excerpt one describes is what I saw in her. The strength of the last sentence, that those eyes would stay etched forever, overpowers the description in two of a sun breaking ice. Both excerpt s are clear and fluent, but Excerpt one carries the emotions of such a moment.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: In that sea-green building which stood like a tired sentinel near Elliot's Beach (where young lovers would soon gather with their smartphones and their dreams, as predictable as the tide), there lived two old men whose synchronicity of existence would have alarmed them had they ever bothered to notice it—but they never did, for such is the peculiar blindness that affects those who are bound together by the invisible threads of fate. The fourth floor (ah, but was it really the fourth? for in this particular building the ground floor was called the first, in the American way, causing endless confusion among visitors and delivery men alike) housed Senior and Junior, names that contained their own little joke, since Junior was himself no spring chicken, and Senior was so ancient that some believed he had witnessed the departure of the British Raj with his own rheumy eyes. Every morning, as predictable as the muezzin's call to prayer that floated across the neighborhood like a ghost's lament, mixing with the timpani of temple bells and the cheerful vulgarity of Tamil film songs blaring from auto-rickshaws, the two men would emerge onto their respective verandas at precisely the same moment, like mechanical figures in some elaborate timepiece. written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The heat arrived early in the day, a simmering, golden haze that crept into the corners of every room, painting the air with a sheen of lethargy. From the fourth floor of a sea-green building, the two men emerged onto their verandas, their movements mirrored as if rehearsed by the stars themselves—Senior and Junior, bound together by the invisible threads of time’s loom. Below, Elliot’s Beach stirred awake, alive with the sounds of its chaotic symphony: temple bells clanged in stubborn competition with film music pouring from distant speakers, a mosaic of devotion and desire. Children’s cries darted through the cacophony like startled birds, while the heady aroma of freshly brewed filter coffee mingled with the briny tang of the sea breeze, a sensory banquet that danced on the edge of overwhelming. Senior adjusted his spectacles, the glint of sunlight catching the lens like a mischievous wink from the heavens, while Junior tapped his fingers on the wrought iron railing, a rhythm only he could hear. Around them, the city moved in fits and bursts: vegetable vendors hollered over their carts, stray dogs wove through scooters with uncanny grace, and the youth, untroubled by time, readied themselves for the evening’s promenade. The two men, unhurried and deliberate, bore witness to it all—custodians of a pace the world had long since abandoned.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: And so the day passed. In the center of the city, the maghrib rang out its ancient melody, warring with the Tamil music lilting out of the speakers of a passing rickshaw—the ocean swell of strings, the buoyant theme of an old Hollywood film. The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. In other neighborhoods, children rendezvoused with their peers in shady alleyways, holding tense diplomatic summits over their games of tag. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: I chose excerpt one because it just made sense to me logically. The flow was better, it was streamed in an order: starting with generic weather, what things looked like around them, and then finally onto the characters. Senior and Junior also were more apart of the story, versus excerpt two where they just like pop up at the end.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
written_by_MFA030.Reason:
The first passage leans too heavily into poetic language that feels very fake or 'for show', which I believe distracts from the core message. The second passage, by contrast, is more straightforward and functional. It focuses on clear details and a tone that lets the scene’s significance speak for itself without having to over-explain or embellish itself, lowering its effectiveness.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The once-vibrant resort now stood in a state of decay, a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region.  The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.

But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.
written_by_MFA032.Reason: There are significant problems with both of these, but I'll say that Excerpt 1 is more fluent and effective, because it succeeds in placing the reader into a sandbox where the point of the narrative is fully absorbed. The reader never questions what is being described, although Excerpt 1 does err in its repetition. It could be condensed. On the other hand, Excerpt 2 alienates the reader by failing to convey the purpose of the setting. The writer evokes purposeless scenes without reference points, leaving the reader confused at times. This means the fluency of Excerpt 1 and its effectiveness are superior.

The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Once gleaming and luxurious, the resort now tells stories of upheaval in every ballroom and courtyard. This resort of yesterday fares poorly today, and no one comes. Beige African sidewalks collect debris, chairs in the European style and English books. A discarded packet of Belga cigarettes transports visitors to another time, allowing them to trespass on the resort in its antebellum years. The whole discarded era becomes visible—Europeans on holiday attempting to make a home of another's home. Visitors may traipse through the relics spilling from sidewalk to grass, walking on both. Now it is a place hung between that past and a present that has not shaken what came before. Children from town tell stories about the resort, what it was and what lives there now: ghosts of both the travelers and the locals who worked in the lobbies and kitchens when the building retained its purpose, ghosts in luxury clothing inappropriate for the climate and ghosts in neatly pressed uniforms. The older teens climb inside through gaps in the boarded windows and explore the detritus, daring each other to venture deeper and deeper down unlit hallways smelling of mold and dust. They speak in whispers. This small entertainment is laced with the petty danger that emanates now from the building. It can be called a harmless thing, a relic of before: before the departures of the whites and the Asians, before independence, before the mutinies. Yet the building, an ugly shell of itself, persists. It says: "But here I still am."
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The resort bore the weight of its past in every crumbling façade and every shattered tile strewn across the once-immaculate promenade. The sidewalks were now a repository for the discarded detritus of another era—splintered furniture, faded paperbacks, and Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot, their familiar logo a ghostly reminder of European elegance. The air, still humid and heavy, carried a vague scent of salt and mildew, mingled with the decay of abandonment. Here, the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow over the resort's decline. Once a haven for settlers who sought to conjure a slice of Europe amidst Africa's heat, it now stood as a relic of disillusionment. The verandas where drinks had clinked under the laughter of expatriates were hollow, their railings stripped of paint, exposing a rusted skeleton beneath.The tide of independence had washed away the veneer of its purpose. Military mutinies had marked its walls with bullet scars; the exodus of the white and Asian populations had left its rooms unclaimed, their emptiness profound. The palm trees swayed in the wind, their silhouettes etched against a bruised sky, but even they seemed tired, their leaves curling at the edges like burnt paper. What once exuded vitality now lay inert, a tableau of exile and loss. The resort, like the colonizers who had built it, was unmoored—a monument to ambitions that had eroded under the weight of history, leaving behind only silence and the memory of what had been.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better in the following ways. Its style is descriptive but in a simpler way that is easier to understand compared to excerpt 2. Its ideas have a more rhythmic flow. It provides a smoother flow in terms of fluency and it communicates its message in a more comprehensive way

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_MFA032.Reason: This one was hard - I think the first excerpt gets at the idea that the father has a new life with a new family better than the second excerpt. The first excerpt is more effective and a touch more fluent than the second excerpt. The second one is more disjointed, especially when it moves from narration to speaking portions.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: At breakfast, my father handed me an envelope thick with cash, a gesture both startling and unsettling. "For Christmas," he said with forced cheer, his eyes flicking toward Chitra, who was sipping her tea, avoiding my gaze. He added, almost apologetically, “And Disney World, with us. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: I like excerpt 1 because it's coherent and follows a clear chronological sequence of events. Overall, excerpt 2 is preferable because it's connected via emotion and metaphor, not just sequence. It uses poetic language, such as "outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything." Excerpt 1 is not as good because it's first person and more repetitive - "I looked," "I tried," "I said."

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind whipped around me, tearing at my clothes and sending the scattered debris dancing across the desolate expanse of the field.  It was a place of stark beauty, where the horizon stretched out like an endless ribbon, and the sky, a vast canvas of swirling greys and blues, mirrored the turmoil within my own heart.For a moment, I allowed myself to be swept away by a fantasy, to imagine that all the things I'd lost in life had somehow washed up here, deposited by the relentless tide of time.  And in that fantastical vision, I saw him, Tommy, his familiar figure emerging from the distant haze, a gentle smile gracing his lips as he waved to me.But I stopped the fantasy before it could take root, before it could weave its way into the fabric of my reality.  The tears came, but I held them back, refusing to let them spill over.  There was a quiet acceptance in that moment, a recognition of the finality of loss. After a while, I turned and walked back to my car, leaving behind the windswept field and the echoes of my fantasy.  The road ahead stretched out before me, a path that I would travel alone, but with a newfound sense of peace.  The world was still there, waiting for me, and life, in all its complexity and beauty, would go on.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 1 is very simple and has short phrases and words which makes it very simple to read, learn and understand. The writer used a very simple choice of words in making the statement complete, hence having a great balance in all forms. It is therefore the best out of the two.

A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better because it it clearly ties the idea of the windy beach with objects washed up on shore to the concept of life being returned. Excerpt 2 starts off with a barren field with trash and then asks the reader to imagine a shore. The transition isn't effective and disrupts the imagery. Excerpt 1 ends positively "Life must go on," but Excerpt 2 ends negatively with "life waiting, indifferent." Both excerpts are fluent, but Excerpt 1 is more coherent and effective.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "Bloody hell! One son a pukka Englishman lawyer, the other a fundamentalist terrorist. I just don't understand it, you raise your children the best you can, but they still grow into strangers."Irie said tentatively, "Oh, that's not true, surely."The disembodied loneliness of the past 20 years collapsed in on Samad as he thought about the state of his family, the state of himself."It's this place. I'm tainted from my time here. I can never go home. I'm from nowhere now, and I'm going nowhere."

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Samad leaned back, fingers tightening around the stem of his glass, watching the amber liquid swirl, gathering his thoughts like a man recalling a half-forgotten dream. "You know, Irie, I did not come here to stay," he began, with the kind of dramatic pause he enjoyed, as if delivering some great revelation. "No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. Her former husband had taken her to such seaside restaurants. But it wasn’t the absence of captured life that stirred in her some unrest but the anticipation of life, of color becoming, the canvas waiting. Even in colorful pockets of her vision–out the deck window to the yellow lampposts and dark ocean–it all bathed in the moon’s white glow. Opaque, the blurred background of a photograph. Yes, a photo, something calling back something that had been. And what of her life now? Why did now pass her as every prior moment had, leaving a feeling, for feelings to be the dropped breadcrumbs of life in its constant evasion? She was struck by an intense nostalgia for Jean-Marc.But how can one feel nostalgia for something — or someone — who sits merely an arm's length away?“Perhaps it’s the grief,” Jean-Marc said. “Your mind is preparing you for loss. Is it not easier to wrap these memories in a protective cloak of nostalgia?”If it was all for impending loss, then her mind was well acquainted. But it wasn’t grief she felt when she thought of her son. She imagined him swinging around the pole of a lamppost. Like breadcrumbs, she happened upon joy in the world’s dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made. Her child was dead. Her husband was gone. Jean-Marc would one day be gone. And yet.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.

We are all familiar with how confusing emotions can be.  This is referenced by "who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions?"  As further stated, emotions "come and go as they please."

written_by_MFA003.Reason: I'm actually torn with this one. Excerpts 1 and 2 feel like very different styles of writing trying to accomplish very different things. Both are good to me depending on the goal of the writer. Except 1 feels languidly grief-stricken and is written in close 3rd with both the pacing and the content matching the spiraling and chaotic nature of the character's thoughts. It feels patchy and jumbled because in close 3rd, the character feels this way. In that sense, I like it. I also am always going to be more drawn to passages that intersperse narration with dialogue; it's simply what I prefer and it makes me more immersed in the scene. So as far as effectiveness, if this is the writer's goal, I find this chaotic and evocative style very compelling. Excerpt 2 is extremely "telling" versus showing, which is not inherently a bad thing (regardless of what creative writing 101 might say), but it certainly gives a lot of distance. Excerpt 2 is distant 3rd person and more straightforward as it describes the character's grief and nostalgia, but I still find the writing beautiful and I could see it working very well for novels of a certain style seeking to evoke a certain feel. It gives the sense of looking down on the scene rather than being immersed in it, and for some stories that can be a relief. An over-reliance on showing at all costs exhausts me as a reader, especially depending on the overall goal and arc of the novel, sometimes a good tell is needed for pacing. So, I chose excerpt 1, but honestly I am inclined to say it's equal to me, depending on context and intent of the author. I like both.

We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The restaurant, awash in the starkness of white – the deck, the table, the lampposts, and even the moon, an orb of paleness in the sky, seemed to mirror the landscape of her emotions.  She was there with Jean-Marc, yet a wave of nostalgia, so intense, so profound, washed over her.  It was a peculiar sensation, this yearning for the past, when the object of her longing was right there beside her.  Jean-Marc, with the uncanny ability to read the intricate map of her heart, understood.  Such nostalgia, he explained, often veiled a deeper fear – the fear of losing a loved one, of a future where they were no longer present. And then, her thoughts drifted to her child, the one she had lost, a wound that had never fully healed.  In that moment, a flicker of happiness, as unexpected as a summer storm, surprised her.  The happiness was fleeting, replaced by a wave of fear at having experienced such a sensation.  It was as if emotions, like wayward children, refused to be tamed, to be told what to feel, when to feel.  We may choose our actions, our words, but feelings, those elusive specters, held sway over the uncharted territories of the heart.  They were the uninvited guests who barged in, the rebels who defied reason, the free spirits who danced to their own tune.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: Longer after leaving her husband, she understood that she should be happy, that this was a moment that called for equanimity: the white linen of the tablecloth under the full moon, lampposts pained white; the waiter with his porcelain platter of oysters on the half-shell, carefully set down before her. Such beautiful, pure things! Yet she was experiencing an odd nostalgia, a longing for this moment even as she sat in her chair within it. She thought the feeling meant: life will never get better than this. The future was her and Jean-Marc, together, but older, and recovered from the mania of fresh love, or perhaps not together at all. But how is it apprpropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her ? (Jean-Marc however had the answer: the more intensely we love someone in the present, the more we grieve their inevitable absence in some imagined future.) But she did not think that was what she meant at all! The mention of death made her think of the child. The child, forever a child, existing without complication in her death. The solidity of this shot her through with pure happiness. She felt afraid; she clasped her hands together in her lap and said nothing more. How easy it is to reign in our words and actions! But then there is always feeling, loping around like an untrained dog inside all of us, aware of how much we long to leash it.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: The two excerpt s above are the hardest for me to separate yet. The first excerpt does build on emotion to portray the characters feelings of love and loss in a somewhat subtle manner, but I again feel that its nuance is lost on the overuse of poetic style and metaphor. The second, however, covers very similar themes in a very similar manner, but is far more straightforward. This may be taken by some as reducing the impact or immersion, but I feel the added coherence and fluency counteracts this, therefore making it a fare more readable and therefore effective piece of writing overall.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt two utilize appropriate punctuation that enables smooth flow and transitions to tell a story. In contrast, excerpt one is choppy and more difficult to follow. In excerpt one the writing incudes many details that are clearly connected to the development of the story while excerpt two includes details that are loosely connected to the story.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti. The process of cooking it was satisfying, but the idea of perfecting it was addictive. Like any dedicated student, I gathered the necessary equipment. I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: There was a time when spaghetti became an obsession, a solitary ritual in my small apartment.  I had this idea that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone, savoring every twirl of the fork, every subtle nuance of the sauce.  It was a dish that demanded solitude, a quiet contemplation of the simple things in life. I had made a pilgrimage to a specialty store, a treasure trove of culinary tools, where I acquired a large pot, a gleaming stainless steel monument to my spaghetti ambitions, and a kitchen timer, its ticking a metronome marking the passage of time until my spaghetti was cooked to perfection.  From supermarkets catering to foreigners, I gathered exotic spices, plump tomatoes, and an assortment of pasta brands, each promising a unique spaghetti experience. My small apartment transformed into a spaghetti laboratory, filled with the rich aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, a fragrant symphony that clung to the curtains, the furniture, even my clothes. I experimented with countless sauces, each simmering on the stove, a testament to my dedication to the art of spaghetti. Sundays marked the beginning of my spaghetti week, a repetitive cycle of cooking and consuming spaghetti, my days revolving around this singular dish.  Tea and a simple salad were the supporting players, but spaghetti was the star, the center around which my culinary world revolved.  There was a comfort in this ritual, a sense of order in the twirling of the spaghetti, the methodical consumption of the dish.Spaghetti Days, I called them, stretching from Sunday to Sunday, a solitary symphony of flavors and textures, a testament to my love affair with this humble dish.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: '...a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there' This anecdote effectively creates imagery of the type of shop the character is in contrasting with "From supermarkets catering to foreigners.." in excerpt 2 which feels more basic. Excerpt 1 uses simple descriptive language effectively vs excerpt 2 which over-relies on more flamboyant language.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: These are both good! I think I like Excerpt 1 better, because it tells more of an emotional story, whereas Excerpt 2 tells a sensory story, but isn't really as effective in portraying *why* the author is making spaghetti. Excerpt 1, on the other hand, is really effective at explaining why the spaghetti ritual has formed, why the author doesn't invite friends over, etc. It paints the routine as a bit sadder than in Excerpt 2, also-- the ritual in Excerpt 1 seems more lonely, whereas in Excerpt 2, the author seems, and even states, that they find the ritual meditative.

I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_MFA003.Reason:
Deciding between the two excerpts was difficult, as they both each tell a different story. One is a short-lived, but passionate, relationship with spaghetti, and the other opens a long-term affair with pasta.
Both excerpts are coherent in their different ways, both have an author who is believable so the words naturally go together with each other, and thirdly both conjure up images of their wildly different kitchens and recipes. I decided to go with the second excerpt, but it may just be because I'm a bit hungry.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: That winter night, my mother told me, was like a blade of ice pressed against her spine. The scissors lay sterilized in boiling water, steam rising like ghostly breath in the dim room, while her trembling hands folded and refolded the small white gown she'd fashioned from scraps in her sewing box. When the pain came, it was not like anything living – it was ancient, prehistoric, like continents being torn apart. She bit down on a rolled cloth, her screams collapsing inward, becoming part of her flesh, part of the darkness. The umbilical cord, when she finally cut it, was purple-blue like twilight, like the last moment before complete darkness. She held the tiny body, so light it could have been made of paper, chanting words that weren't words but rather the sound of her soul trying to transfer its own life force. For one heartbeat, maybe two, the baby's chest rose – a movement so slight it could have been the shadow of hope itself. Then stillness. The floor's cold crept up through her body like rising water, until she too became still, became ice, became the very essence of winter itself. Her warmth retreated inward, as though trying to follow her child into that place beyond reaching.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Both excerpt s are vivid, but the first excerpt requires more imagination to visualize the scene. It is more descriptive and uses figurative language better- "like a blade of ice pressed against her spine." The excerpt is gut-wrenching and heartbreaking and does well with getting its point across to the reader.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: It was a winter morning thick with silence, the kind that stretches across frozen earth, hollow and unforgiving. My mother knelt on the cold wooden floor, her breath visible in the brittle air as she arranged the meager preparations she could muster. A pot of water on the stove, its steam curling upward like the last prayers of the desperate, her trembling hands struggling with scissors dulled by time. In the dim light, the pale fabric she had cut into a crude gown seemed to shiver, as though alive with the sorrow that filled the room. Pain ripped through her body like a jagged knife, forcing her onto her knees, but her face, pale and drawn, bore the stoic determination of someone who knew that the world would not offer her mercy. The moment of birth arrived, primal and raw, a soundless rupture of the fragile divide between life and death. She held the newborn close, her whispered pleas breaking against the unyielding silence. "Live," she murmured, a chant that carried the weight of her being. For one fragile heartbeat, the child stirred, its existence fleeting, a candle flickering in a relentless wind. Then it was gone, leaving behind only its weightless absence. My mother sat there, cradling the lifeless form, her own warmth seeping into the icy floor. The stillness settled over her like a shroud, and in that moment, the world outside ceased to exist.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Both excerpt 1 and excerpt 2 are effective at telling the sorrow story. Excerpt 1 takes a more poetic approach while excerpt 2 is written in a more straight forward manner. The poetic prose of excerpt one prevents it from having smooth writing that flows together, yet still achieves the same effectiveness as excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Reason: I felt that both excerpt s were coherent.  Probably equally so.  The fluency in both was similar as well, however I did feel that some of the sentences in excerpt 2 were a little wordy and diminished the quality of the description at times.  They could have been broken up into two sentences, or they were not necessary at all. I think this affected the effectiveness of he excerpt for me, which made excerpt 1 a better choice for me to clearly understand what was being said.
