written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Charles de Gaulle Airport, where the Parisian winter raged outside, a vision of timeless beauty emerged amidst the sterile expanse of the terminal.  A striking woman, her skin kissed by the sun like ancient amber, her eyes pools of liquid obsidian, moved with the grace of a lioness through the bustling crowd.  A flowing, emerald-green kaftan draped her form, its edges embroidered with intricate symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations.  A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: excerpt  one was too confusing and distracting from the beginning I had to read and reread several times to organize the words in my head. The words felt as if they were physically placed one by one as compared to excerpt two which has a smoother flow. Much more engaging.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better written and more understandable. Excerpt 1 feels cumbersome to understand. It feels like an attempt to show intelligence and not an attempt to communicate. Sun-dappled, centuries of whispers and spring-a contradiction are all terms that make excerpt 1 difficult to read. The writing of course is understandable but difficult to.

She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 1 is needlessly verbose with the man's observation of the woman. Excerpt 2 still hits on her beauty but no need to spend so much time on it, it doesn't offer any extra feeling to the reader. The reader understands she is beautiful. Also the flip to the observation of GDG airport is a bit jarring in excerpt 1 but fits nicely with the introduction in excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.

The language used depicts the emotion of the event happening, the state of the character in question. An example from the excerpt is “there is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind.”

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The lingering image of Robbie and Cecilia, their figures receding down the driveway into the white mist, remains etched in my memory. It's a scene I've revisited countless times, a reminder of the love I shattered and the atonement I sought through my writing. In the twilight of my life, I question the nature of truth. Is a merciful fabrication, a crafted illusion of happiness, a greater kindness than the stark reality of a love tragically cut short? Robbie likely succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes. Cecilia perished in Balham Underground station during a bombing raid. Their letters lie preserved in a war museum, a testament to a love forever unfulfilled. Yet, in my final act of creation, I dared to defy fate. I granted them a reprieve, a fictional sanctuary where their love survived. It was a rebellion against the relentless march of time and tragedy. As the shadows lengthen, I wonder if I was right to weave this tapestry of hope. Would they have preferred the stark truth, the bitter knowledge of their unfulfilled love? Or is it a greater kindness to let them live on in my fictional world, forever young, forever in love? The question lingers, unresolved, like an echo in my mind. Perhaps there is no right answer to this age-old dilemma. Perhaps the truth, like beauty, lies in the eye of the beholder. A hopeful ending, even if untrue, is a more fitting tribute to their love than the harsh reality of their tragic fate.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? At the edge of her fading strength, she allowed herself the faintest smile, perhaps at last, a merciful fiction was the highest form of kindness.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.

Like how a dying premier's eyes go all WhatThe? and BetYouFeelBadNow. Like how the headlines say Justice Served! while your brain screams MurderGuy! MurderGuy! at 3 A.M. But this new premier? Total sicko. Made the last one look like a Kindness Enhancement Specialist. The way those thick-necked guards stood around him at press conferences, all We'reNotThinkingAboutGunsUnderOurJackets. Could go on TV, start a movement: Area Man Admits to Double-Premier Elimination, Seeks Followers. The old him, Pre-Premier-Removal him, would've just gone home, watched GameShows™. But that guy? That guy was dead as Uncle Pete. He grabbed the door handle, feeling that old familiar Here-We-Go-Again tingle. Time to make history. Again.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The red car was old, a wheezing relic. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? Murder wasn’t a thing you could just stop doing like sugar or carbs. It left its hooks in you, lodged under the ribs, twisting whenever you tried to breathe easy. The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. And for what? A better world? Please. The world had gone on, more evil, more absurd. The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it? To step into the role, a public avenger, claim the credit, lead the charge? But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one. That thought sickened him. No. Obscurity was the real death. He flung the door open, the cold air a slap. Time to go.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.

Excerpt 1 has some sentence structure issues and would benefit from better word choice.

Excerpt two conjures more images in my head when I read it with the use of descriptive language. It also flows more smoothly - you can sense his distress and uncertainty through the slower pace used to describe his thoughts: '...This was justice, wasn’t it?...' and: '...But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one...'

The adjective choice in excerpt one makes me think the author has no qualms doing what he's about to do: '...bouncing off against the car...' and: '...making the red paint seem redder...' It's urgent, dangerous, passionate - the author feels he has no choice but to murder and is fine with it. That the uncle's death is mentioned in such a blasé way alongside the sounds his ghost makes implies the author isn't bothered by death, it's just another part of life: '...making woosh-whee-whooo sounds...' His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: I visit my father and immediately notice new changes. The way he holds his coffee cup with both hands now, like a child. The way his eyes move around the room without settling. When I ask about his work, he stares at the wall behind me. My mother quickly fills the silence: "Tell her about your writing on the Bible, dear. The anti-Semitism research." He nods, but I can see he's already forgotten the prompt. "I'm proud of you," he says to me suddenly, then adds, "though I have nothing to say." I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance. Later, my mother pulls me aside to show me a photograph. "Look," she says, "this was forty years ago." In it, my father stands straight-backed beside a podium, papers spread before him like fallen leaves. I notice how his collar sits perfectly against his neck, how his hands rest purposefully on the wooden edge. My mother's fingers tremble slightly as she returns the photo to its drawer. I think: This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: My father, a stranger in his own house, sits hunched in his armchair, a shadow of the man I knew.  His eyes, once bright and full of life, are now clouded with confusion.  He struggles to remember what he's working on, a question met with a sigh and a shake of his head.  My mother, her face etched with worry, reminds him gently, "Your writing, dear, on the Bible and anti-Semitism."  A flicker of recognition crosses his face, a brief spark in the fading embers of his mind.He looks at me, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.  "My daughter," he says, his voice a fragile whisper, "so proud of you."  But the light fades quickly, replaced by a vacant stare.  "Nothing to say," he murmurs, lost in the labyrinth of his own thoughts.  The silence that follows is heavy, filled with unspoken words and a growing sense of loss.Later, my mother shows me a photograph from forty years ago.  My father, young and vibrant, stands with his arm around her, both of them radiating joy.  My mother's voice cracks as she speaks, her words laced with a quiet despair.  "It's like he's already gone," she says, her eyes filled with tears.  I look at the photograph again, the image of my father frozen in time, a stark contrast to the frail figure sitting in the other room.  The weight of his absence, even in his presence, settles over me, a heavy cloak of sorrow that I cannot shake off.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. My mother told him this. “Your work,” she said. “You’ve been writing about the Bible.” He nodded, as if this was something he could accept, though not something he quite believed. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 has a clearer and more coherent description of the course of events that happened and also used more direct dialogue to establish more emotional connections such as 'I have nothing to say to you' whereas excerpt 2 mentions this in passing without using dialogue which reduces the effectiveness.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.

I like the flow of #2 as well, as it brings memories of my own dead, and those that I remember in similar ways, so I can commiserate with the way of thinking that the narrator is using.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The air in the apartment is heavy, thick with the scent of lilies and the ghost of his presence.  Time, that relentless tide, keeps moving, yet I seem stranded, caught in the undertow of grief.  It's been a year and four months since John, my John, slipped through the veil, and the world insists on reminding me.The calendar, that cruel arbiter of time, mocks me with its relentless march forward.  Each day is a faded echo of the one before, a year removed.  I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.Yesterday, I crossed Lexington Avenue, the same way I've done a thousand times before.  But this time, it was different.  This time, I carried the weight of December 31, 2003, a date that exists in my world but not in his.  It was the day he ceased to be, the day the world shifted on its axis.And in that moment, I realized the terrible truth.  We who are left behind, we try to keep the dead alive in our memories, clinging to their fading essence like a lifeline.  But in doing so, we create a purgatory, a liminal space where they are neither here nor there.  To truly live, to move forward, we must keep them dead.  It's a harsh reality, a bitter pill to swallow.  But it's the only way to navigate the treacherous terrain of grief.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: When I think of John now, whether in grief or joy, time makes a mirage of our parting. Memories are distant, those vibrant, vivid images inevitably softened by the passing days and nights into muddy and distorted reflections. My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. When he was alive, who did we see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then? Crossing Lexington Avenue in the wintry haze enveloping New York, a cold, damp curtain hung above the city, I come across the date—December 31, 2003—and realize John never saw this day last year. My exercise for keeping time has expired, and my husband lives in the distant past. I might transplant him here, invite him as memory into this moment to maintain our profound connection, the sort unsevered by death so long as he is kept within the perfect safety of memory. Yet it occurs to me—in this exercise of resurrection, I am only ensuring that I, too, never see December 31, 2003. That I, like John, live only in my recollections. Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash falls down the curtain, a pallid crescent in the gloom of the room.  I can hear the ticking of the watch, a steady pulse in the quiet.  It was Grandfather’s watch, and now it is Father’s, and someday it will be mine.  The watch ticks on, a metronome marking the inexorable passage of time.  Father said, “You cannot conquer time.  You can only try to forget it.”  But how can one forget time when it is always there, ticking away, a constant reminder of our mortality?  The watch hands move, a slow, relentless dance towards the end.  “Time is a relentless and hungry force,” Father said.  “It devours all things – youth, beauty, even memory.”  The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives.  Each tick brings us closer to the end, to the final silence.  “Victories in life are fleeting,” Father said.  “They are but illusions in the face of time’s infinite and hungry maw.”  The watch ticks on, a constant reminder of our mortality.  It is a sound that haunts me, a sound that echoes the futility of our existence.  “Jesus walking on Galilee,” Father said, “and Saint Francis, speaking to his Little Sister Death.  Both of them knew that time could not be conquered, that it could only be endured.”  The watch ticks on, a steady beat in the silence of the room.  It is a sound that I cannot escape, a sound that reminds me of my own mortality.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass hung cinched by the dark of the sash. It stood unstirred in the limpid bedroom air. No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age. My grandfather’s watch–which still belonged to my father even after his death as dogs belong to their buried owners, circling their grave and howling the premonitions my grandfather had uttered in his own bed: life being one big fever dream, all its hills and troughs in one fell swoop wrenched from under you, a dream from which you will be wrenched, and you wake in the unending dark where you take no triumphs with you, and the ceaseless hounds of timestamp flat your burial mound and the sky’s days pass beyond–ticked incessantly somewhere in the dark. My father talked about the dark in a similar night’s stifled room. How Saint Francis welcomed Little Sister Death as the dark all around Jesus when he walked along the long and lonely light-rays. Beyond that dark is nothing but dark, that we only know dark from the little light we got. We only know time because we count it, but countless time goes unticked in the unending dark, so much time there is no before, no after, the unnumbered breezes with no curtain to shape them. No, my time is never truly had. I felt the air too thick to breathe.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt one is better than excerpt 2 because it was able to give a distinct and interesting story between reality and imagination, making us live in this imagination as reality. It was more engaging and smooth. Excerpt 2 was engaging but not as smooth in writing as the excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. He paid his considerable rent to the Sanderson family without hesitation, never noticing how quickly they pocketed the money, as though it might carry some taint of the house itself. In his hotel room, preparing for his first night in Hill House, he arranged his instruments with precise care - thermometers, cameras, tape recorders - tools of rationality to measure the irrational. He did not yet understand that Hill House had been waiting for him, had perhaps called to him through all his years of searching, and that his arrival was merely the beginning of what the house had planned, as it stood against its hills, patient and hungry, its doors sensibly shut against the approaching night.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.  For eighty years it had borne silent witness to untold horrors, and eighty more it might endure, its walls upright, its floors firm, its doors closed, a tomb of secrets.  Within its depths, Dr. John Montague, a man of letters and a scholar of the unseen, sought to unravel the mysteries that clung to the house like cobwebs.  His excitement was a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed beneath his skin as he surveyed his conquest.He had come seeking a haunted house, and Hill House, with its malevolent reputation, seemed to fit the bill.  It had cost him dearly, this pursuit of the paranormal, both in the coin of the realm and the currency of his reputation.Yet, he was undeterred, his resolve as firm as the foundations of the house itself.  He would have his proof, his definitive study of psychic disturbances, a testament to the unseen world that whispered just beyond the veil of perception. Dr. Montague, a man who clung to his title as if it were a life raft in a sea of skepticism, was determined to conquer the mysteries of Hill House.  He would face the darkness, the unseen forces that lurked within, and emerge with the truth, or be consumed by the shadows that stretched long and hungry within the walls of the house.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.

The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 2 has better flow and explains the significance of the house more than excerpt 1 does which is important to the reader understanding the premise of the story. Excerpt 2 is more coherent and fluent for the reader as the passage flows from thought to though where Excerpt 1 skips back and forth between concepts.

written_by_MFA022.Excerpt1: Dr. John Montague stood before Hill House, a place that loomed as though waiting, its cold stones heavy with silence. The house, not sane, appeared to lean slightly forward, its dark windows watching him with a lifeless gaze, as though withholding secrets that could never be pried free. Hill House had stood for eighty years, holding within its walls an impenetrable darkness that even sunlight seemed reluctant to touch. The hills rose sharply behind it, framing its stark isolation; the house seemed less built than grown, an aberration of nature. Dr. Montague, meticulous in his methods yet quietly burdened by self-doubt, adjusted his glasses, a gesture as habitual as his reliance on his title—"Doctor of Philosophy in Anthropology"—to shield himself from skepticism. For years, his inquiries into the supernatural had been met with thinly veiled disdain, but Hill House represented his long-sought grail: an authentic haunting, a house with whispers in its foundation. He had rented the property at a steep price, its rooms and halls offered not for comfort but as a proving ground for his theories. As he crossed the threshold, the air seemed to shift, pressing lightly against his skin as though the house was tasting him. He paused, glancing back at the gravel drive that led away, the thought fleeting: nothing here would let him leave unmarked. The door shut behind him with a finality that echoed briefly, then faded, swallowed entirely by the unbroken, unnerving silence of Hill House.
written_by_MFA022.Excerpt2: Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness. A house born within a garden of oleander, no person alive could claim witness to its birth, and so the poisonous intentions of the house were known only to itself. Only Dr. Montague, snaking up the thorn-lined driveway in a car packed with books, would observe the house’s final blooming, though even he, a man of scholarship and philosophy, a fastidious believer in the supernatural, would come to doubt what the Hill House had to show him. Dr. Montague was a man of doubt, not of the world, or of the unspoken phenomena hidden within it, but of himself, and his instincts, which he sought to justify through scholarship; Indeed, he arrived at Hill House surrounded by the false safety of his books on an errand of study, having rented the home at considerable personal and financial cost, with the hope of producing definitive work on psychic disturbances and their accompanying phenomena. He believed himself, after conducting a lifelong search for a haunted home, to have found Hill House; this was a false belief. It was Hill House that found Dr. Montague, alone in his study, nursing his failures with cognac in hand as he lingered over a newspaper clipping which happened to mention, offhandedly, the strange occurrences of a mansion atop a hill in a small New England town. This home could contain answers, he thought, slowing his car to park beneath the ominous gaze of the house's front windows, answers only I can find.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: My husband’s plan, while shame-inducing, worked. The master of the house believed I was Kevin’s slave, not his wife. I felt awkward around the house’s slaves. I’d tasted a freedom they would never see. Our only threat was Margaret, who seemed to notice that something was amiss. She could tell that we slept together, but a master taking a slave to bed was normal enough — Margaret was all too familiar with that. But perhaps she could tell that we didn’t belong in her era. We awaited that dangerous revelation for some time, but it never came. My work was bland, as was Kevin’s new social life. He always wanted a break despite never having to work. “I think, maybe,” he said, tossing an apple up and down as I cleaned, “we should get out of here. Explore. Visit the west? We could meet a real cowboy!” “So you suggest being nothing more than tourists? As my ancestors stay enslaved in the south? As the natives in the west are exploited?” I felt my voice shifting, becoming sharper, ready to stab. “We’ve traveled through time. Maybe we ought to change history.” Kevin contemplated my outburst, thoughtful but unemotional. “A tempting idea, but we shouldn’t interfere,” he said casually, bit into his apple, and left the room. I scrubbed away at the floor angrily. In this time, and even in our own, his life was made easier by history proceeding exactly as it had. Of course he didn’t want anything to change.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The shame burned in my throat, a sour taste I couldn't swallow. Here I was, in this house, in this time, a part of this… this obscenity. Kevin beside me, and us both belonging to a man who thought us less than human.Margaret, with her sly smiles and knowing glances, she was a threat, I knew it. But not the normal kind, not the kind that would have Kevin bedding down with the master. No, this was something different, something more insidious.The days blurred, one into the next. The work, surprisingly, wasn't the hard part. It was the waiting, the knowing, the constant awareness of our place here. Kevin, bless his heart, seemed to find it all rather romantic. "Imagine," he'd say, his eyes alight, "exploring the West, seeing the cowboys and Indians."I'd just stare at him, the bile rising in my throat. "Cowboys and Indians," I'd scoff, "more like thieves and the stolen. While we're chained here in the South, they're out West taking land that never belonged to them."He'd frown, his romantic notions shattered. "It's not the same," he'd argue, "they're not slaves.""No," I'd retort, "but they're not free either. Not when their land is being taken, their way of life destroyed."He'd sigh, the conversation turning sour, as it always did. We were in this together, but we saw it so differently. He, with his head in the clouds, romanticizing the past. Me, with my feet on the ground, seeing the ugliness for what it was.

Excerpt 2 is more engaging and flows naturally making the reader glued to the story. This makes excerpt 2 better in quality as compared to excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: After our fourth week on the plantation, what had begun as horrifying became mundane. The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. On a Friday afternoon, Kevin snuck by to make small talk. “I never thought I would see you folding napkins at a dining table.” What the hell was wrong with him? I seethed back, “Do you think I’m doing this for any other reason than my survival?” He replied, “Well, of course not. But I don’t exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master’s errand boy either.” Before I could interject to explain the mortal difference between indentured servitude and slavery, he went on to say, “We should escape, take advantage of this insanity, and see things people in our time dream of. I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. The fieldhand slaves outside generate the profits that the master reaps from the government. The government will use his raw goods to wipe out entire bloodlines of Lakota, Sioux, and countless other tribes. And in 200 years, white men will let their imaginations run wild in the lands their great-great-grandfathers slaughtered empty.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.

Fluency is there with the use of a range of descriptive language, metaphors and similes which brings the text to life for the reader. Overall, an effective piece with excellent sentence starters.

Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better because is more focused and emotionally grounded, feels like you are sitting in the moment with them, with line like " while you dream of cowboys... says much without overexplaining while excerpt 1 has strong ideas but do too much, it throws a lot at once. excerpt 2 keeps it clear without losing its weight.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: After our fourth week on the plantation, what had begun as horrifying became mundane. The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. On a Friday afternoon, Kevin snuck by to make small talk. “I never thought I would see you folding napkins at a dining table.” What the hell was wrong with him? I seethed back, “Do you think I’m doing this for any other reason than my survival?” He replied, “Well, of course not. But I don’t exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master’s errand boy either.” Before I could interject to explain the mortal difference between indentured servitude and slavery, he went on to say, “We should escape, take advantage of this insanity, and see things people in our time dream of. I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. The fieldhand slaves outside generate the profits that the master reaps from the government. The government will use his raw goods to wipe out entire bloodlines of Lakota, Sioux, and countless other tribes. And in 200 years, white men will let their imaginations run wild in the lands their great-great-grandfathers slaughtered empty.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: The excerpt is a vivid explanation which exposes Kevin as an individual who is ready to explore a new land, but assumes that the residents in the area are not economically using the available land. The coherency of the excerpt makes us reflect on the historical period of exploration. A statement like "do you think they want explorers ..." is a clear indicator that the excerpt is effective and fluent in terms of how the ideas are presented, and how they flow from the beginning.

written_by_MFA031.Reason: While the speed of Excerpt 2 is engaging, it is Excerpt 1 that has the strongest writing quality. Reasoning being is that Excerpt 1 achieves its goal by telling us the setting ("plantation") and makes clear that the characters are on a plantation. This gives the reader an idea of what year this might be placed in, and what the setting might look like (for readers who are familiar with what plantations looked like). It's also clear that both Kevin and the narrator are slaves in Excerpt 1: "But I don't exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master's errand boy either (Kevin)" and "Do you think I'm doing this for any other reason than my own survival" (narrator) in combination with "...what had begun as horrifying became mundane" (narrator) helps to make immediately clear that both are unwillingly in this position of slavery. Whereas Excerpt 2 is confusing, it's unclear what is going on with the characters: "...Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?" (narrator). This leads the reader to wonder if Kevin and the narrator are explorers as this is the narrator's response to Kevin and if they are not, it lacks a reason to be in the text. Due to this, it reads unnaturally, which causes it to lack fluency, and this confusion of wondering what the setting is, who the characters are, and what the problem is, leads to a lack of coherence. However, Excerpt 1 does an excellent job at coherence. Kevin explains that he wants to escape, makes clear that he wants to explore the Wild West, and creates a point of tension in the narrative in doing so (building its effectiveness).

The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. On a Friday afternoon, Kevin snuck by to make small talk. “I never thought I would see you folding napkins at a dining table.” What the hell was wrong with him? I seethed back, “Do you think I’m doing this for any other reason than my survival?” He replied, “Well, of course not. But I don’t exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master’s errand boy either.” Before I could interject to explain the mortal difference between indentured servitude and slavery, he went on to say, “We should escape, take advantage of this insanity, and see things people in our time dream of. I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. The fieldhand slaves outside generate the profits that the master reaps from the government. The government will use his raw goods to wipe out entire bloodlines of Lakota, Sioux, and countless other tribes.
