written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.

Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.

That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be").Excerpt 2 builds a sense of apprehension and dread, from its references to the overseers making life miserable for the toilers on the plantation ("Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn't help"), to the pointed question asked of Kevin ("Untamed for who?"). In contrast, Excerpt 1 seems to hail from a bigger picture sort of perspective (such as the bitter prediction of its final sentence), which a reader may -- or may not need -- right away.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Reva seemed distant the last time we talked, though maybe I’m just imagining that now. She was breathing heavily into the phone when she picked up. It sounded like she was having sex, and I made a mean joke about it, and she laughed in a forced way and told me she was at the gym, on the elliptical, which I could imagine easily, her in that ugly little workout set, climbing toward nothing. She told me she’d call me back later, but she never did. Then she went missing after 9/11, and I knew she was dead. Not in any kind of mystical or spiritual way, but because I knew there was no other option. That same day, I bought a TV/VCR from Best Buy with cash because I wanted to record the news coverage. Now, I watch it, not in a morbid way, but hoping I’ll find a clue, about something, maybe about Reva, maybe about something else. It’s not about Trevor anymore. He’s in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably slathering sunscreen on his anorexic wife and pretending to be happy. Or maybe he is happy. I was watching one of the recordings today when I spotted something. From the smoking North Tower, a woman poked her torso out of a window. She was wearing a blue sweater and jeans. She had brown hair, short like Reva’s. She hovered on the edge for a moment, then let go and plunged into the unknown. She sailed weightlessly through the air, and then she disappeared out of frame.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I'd stared at my cheap TV/VCR combo for hours that day, recording endless footage while sprawled on my beige couch, still warm from my body's perpetual indent. The towers fell again and again on my screen – I'd rewind, watch, rewind, watch, like some demented projectionist in a theater of one. Reva had called from her gym that morning, rambling about calories and men and whatever else filled her anxious mind. I'd barely listened, picking at a hangnail until it bled. Now she was gone, vanished into that cloud of debris and paperwork and human ash that coated lower Manhattan like toxic snow. Trevor was in Barbados with his new wife, probably slathering on coconut-scented sunscreen while I watched people jump from burning buildings. But there was one woman who caught my eye, her body arcing through the air with such grace, such impossible beauty, that I felt a sick surge of envy. She looked like Reva – same dark hair, same slight build – but she moved like a dancer, like she'd chosen this terrible performance. I watched her fall hundreds of times, memorizing the way her skirt billowed, how her arms stretched wide as if embracing the sky. She became my obsession, this falling angel in sensible office wear. I understood her choice in a way that frightened me. There was something pure in it, something almost holy – to leap into nothingness rather than wait for it to claim you. I never told anyone how much I admired her courage.

These thoughts are like one scene leading to another: the clumsy telephone conversation, the inevitability of the death of Reva, the acquisition of the TV/VCR, the ritualistic viewing, and the eventual realization of the falling woman. There is no sense of something attachable or decorative. The thoughts of the narrator are like actual memory, moving associatively, but within control. The thoughts in the excerpt 2 are clearer, though more piled up more aggressively. The emotional endings (envy, admiration, holiness) come so fast and so forcefully, which somewhat diminishes the psychological adventure rather than allowing it to flourish.
Fluency:
The first excerpt is more natural to read. Rhythms of the sentences are different without making much emphasis, and the language used seems natural and not artificial. Even biting edges, such as "climbing toward nothing," slip in monotonously and hang. Excerpt 2 reads fluently in a technical way; however, it is heavy-handed in heightened phrasing and repetition. The prose even gives warning of its intensity, rather than allowing it to emerge naturally, which can make the voice feel more self-aware.
Effectiveness:
It is in this area where excerpt 1 triumphs. It appears to aim at disturbing the reader with its lack of judgment and explanation--and it achieves it. The narrator does not give us any instructions on how we should feel about the woman who fell; we are forced to sit and perceive the unsettling ambiguity. Excerpt 2 is an emotionally potent piece of writing, but it expounds its point too explicitly. The termination of the fall as pure, holy, and courageous is an attempt to reduce the ability of the reader to interpret what is going on, and this makes the haunting element of the moment somewhat less convincing.

Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: I stared at the television screen, the pixelated image of the Twin Towers collapsing, a grotesque loop of destruction playing over and over.  Reva, my dear Reva, was lost in the chaos, her voice a distant echo on the other end of a dropped phone call."Are you there?" I had asked, the dial tone buzzing in my ear.Hours earlier, the news had crackled to life, the blue glow of the television illuminating the room.  Trevor was away in Barbados, his honeymoon a cruel irony in the face of the unfolding tragedy.  I watched the towers crumble, the smoke billowing, a woman leaping from the inferno, her body a fragile arc against the backdrop of the burning sky. "She looks like Reva," I whispered, a strange sense of admiration washing over me.The woman's beauty, even in the face of death, was mesmerizing. Her courage, her desperation, her final act of defiance against the inevitable.I watched her fall, the image burned into my mind, a haunting reminder of the fragility of life.Reva, my wild, untamed friend, was gone, swallowed by the chaos, her laughter and vibrancy extinguished.  I mourned her loss, the emptiness a gaping hole in my soul.Days turned into weeks, the world a blur of muted colors and hollow sounds.  I watched the footage repeatedly, the woman's fall a morbid fascination, a symbol of our collective mortality.  In her final act, I saw a reflection of my own struggles, my own search for meaning in a world that often felt meaningless.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Similar to the previous example, despite the use of a wider vocabulary, Excerpt 2 falls short on it's cohernce to tell a quality story, I was much more drawn in by Excerpt 1 and it's ability to be relatable and slightly surprising in it's vocabulary. It was much more enjoyable and relateable in its fluency. These things came together to show Excerpt 1 as a much more effective potrayal of the same story and overall a better quality passage.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Orin woke up next to the subject, mentally flaying himself for referring to this person as such, but using the same voice to berate himself that he used to describe this person as a subject, so the whole process became moot. The sheets were wrinkled and covered in little hairs, and Orin flinched as he recalled a dream of something cliche and horrid, spiders, heights, things rational only to the extent that they pose fear of what you can’t control (the venom, gravity,) and perhaps what you can (being a place with heights or spiders at all). The subject roused and pantomimed closeness, holding Orin’s clammy ribs, giggling at nothing, suggesting they fry or filet or bake the byproducts of various animals for breakfast. Orin’s beady little button eyes shimmered the reflections of the Subject's own eyes, through which they saw, perhaps, a glimpse of their own happiness, their own attempts at it, their own failures towards it. Orin longed to be alone, to return to his routines. Four coffees, each more burned than the last, a shower where he contemplated cleaning the mold spots that grew imperceptibly over the evening, perceptibly over the month, and perhaps a run after to justify the next day’s shower. But he knew that all of it, the loneliness, the mundane, was just a steep climb towards something crested and flat, a plain he wished to never see.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. The whole morning routine thing becoming this desperate assemblage of shields — the multiple coffees and showers and runs — against whatever nameless thing the dreams have excavated in him, and the presence of these "Subjects" (which is exactly the kind of clinically distant terminology someone would use when they're terrified of actual connection) only amplifies the awareness of his own emotional vacancy, which then of course makes him feel even more alienated, which then makes him need more coffee, etc., ad infinitum. That there's something almost liturgical about how he processes these mornings, these rituals of purification that never quite purify. The dreams themselves being less about actual spiders or heights than about the sensation of being watched while being alone, which is possibly the most contemporary form of existential terror there is. And it's worth noting that even in his solitude he's performing for some imagined audience, his anxiety itself becoming a kind of entertainment, the way everything does in our self-conscious age, even our own private sufferings being transformed into these sort of avant-garde performances for audiences that don't exist.

The subject roused and pantomimed closeness, holding Orin’s clammy ribs, giggling at nothing, suggesting they fry or filet or bake the byproducts of various animals for breakfast. Orin’s beady little button eyes shimmered the reflections of the Subject's own eyes, through which they saw, perhaps, a glimpse of their own happiness, their own attempts at it, their own failures towards it. Orin longed to be alone, to return to his routines. Four coffees, each more burned than the last, a shower where he contemplated cleaning the mold spots that grew imperceptibly over the evening, perceptibly over the month, and perhaps a run after to justify the next day’s shower. But he knew that all of it, the loneliness, the mundane, was just a steep climb towards something crested and flat, a plain he wished to never see.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Orin wakes up feeling miserable. It’s always the same thing for him, that feeling of being wrenched out of a bottomless pit, the spiders, the heights, the tsunamis, the teeth falling out and clattering to the floor, the cliché and the boilerplate, dreams and fears so ordinary and yet completely destabilizing. He wants to go through his ritual, the multiple black coffees and the boiling hot shower and the run around the block in his sweatpants, just to get to a state resembling normalcy. But on this particular day, he has woken up next to a Subject, and he feels that rage, at the person he was last night, and also at the person lying in bed beside him. He has been doing this more and more lately, finding somebody to go to bed with, and he always hates himself for it. He wants to go back to the heights and the spiders to avoid the cuddling, the mindless small talk, the fried eggs, the depressing attempts at morning sex, the way the Subjects are chronically unable to recognize his torment. When he is alone, he feels suffocated, but with the Subjects, it’s worse. He wants to go back to the tall building he was teetering on the edge of the moment before he woke up, though now he feels, strangely, like he is already there. The subject rolls over and Orin imagines himself losing balance on that building, and tumbling through the agonizing, nauseating remainder of a lonely and empty day.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Orin awoke in the cold post-dream anxiety and discomfort of a spider’s web, a fall from a height, a suffocating loss of control.  The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering.  Even multiple coffees, showers, or a morning run could barely rinse him of the feeling of being spectacularly tiny and yet at the mercy of something vast and unknowable.  Waking up alone was bad enough, but waking up with a Subject—an overnight guest whose name and details were best left unscrutinized—was a special kind of hell.The Subject, oblivious to the roiling psychic storm within him, would engage in the usual banalities of morning—the vapid small talk, the cuddling, the attempts at cooking breakfast.  Orin would lie there, trapped beneath the weight of their normalcy, feeling like a creature from another dimension.  Their cheerful voices sounded like the chirping of alien insects; their well-meaning touches were suffocating him.  Even when alone, these mornings were a bleak and desolate landscape.  The day stretched before him like a vertical climb or a fall, depending on the dream’s residue.  Either way, it was an ordeal to be endured, a performance to be staged.  The world was a stage, and he was a fraud—a fraud who longed for authenticity but found himself perpetually trapped in the performance of it.  The irony was not lost on him, but neither was it a source of amusement. It was simply a fact, as bleak and inescapable as the morning itself.

This plays the story in a broken form in this readers mind, the story is not fluent because of this road blocks. Excerpt 1 was so easy to consume and the message was put across efficiently.

He wants to go through his ritual, the multiple black coffees and the boiling hot shower and the run around the block in his sweatpants, just to get to a state resembling normalcy. But on this particular day, he has woken up next to a Subject, and he feels that rage, at the person he was last night, and also at the person lying in bed beside him. He has been doing this more and more lately, finding somebody to go to bed with, and he always hates himself for it. He wants to go back to the heights and the spiders to avoid the cuddling, the mindless small talk, the fried eggs, the depressing attempts at morning sex, the way the Subjects are chronically unable to recognize his torment. When he is alone, he feels suffocated, but with the Subjects, it’s worse. He wants to go back to the tall building he was teetering on the edge of the moment before he woke up, though now he feels, strangely, like he is already there. The subject rolls over and Orin imagines himself losing balance on that building, and tumbling through the agonizing, nauseating remainder of a lonely and empty day.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Orin awoke in the cold post-dream anxiety and discomfort of a spider’s web, a fall from a height, a suffocating loss of control.  The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering.  Even multiple coffees, showers, or a morning run could barely rinse him of the feeling of being spectacularly tiny and yet at the mercy of something vast and unknowable.  Waking up alone was bad enough, but waking up with a Subject—an overnight guest whose name and details were best left unscrutinized—was a special kind of hell.The Subject, oblivious to the roiling psychic storm within him, would engage in the usual banalities of morning—the vapid small talk, the cuddling, the attempts at cooking breakfast.  Orin would lie there, trapped beneath the weight of their normalcy, feeling like a creature from another dimension.  Their cheerful voices sounded like the chirping of alien insects; their well-meaning touches were suffocating him.  Even when alone, these mornings were a bleak and desolate landscape.  The day stretched before him like a vertical climb or a fall, depending on the dream’s residue.  Either way, it was an ordeal to be endured, a performance to be staged.  The world was a stage, and he was a fraud—a fraud who longed for authenticity but found himself perpetually trapped in the performance of it.  The irony was not lost on him, but neither was it a source of amusement. It was simply a fact, as bleak and inescapable as the morning itself.

I think 2 just has the edge for shorter sentences that make it a bit easier to read that 1 and so may be more effective.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Orin’s mornings often began as a kind of existential residue, the aftermath of dreams that seemed to gnaw their way out from the deep recesses of the psyche’s cellar, dreams that were equal parts spiders and sheer verticality, both suffocating and vertiginous. The mornings required ritual, regimented almost to the point of ceremony: coffee brewed to a darkness that could rival the void, showers so scalding they left his skin reddened, runs that turned his lungs into bellows just to remind himself he was alive. Yet the presence of a Subject—the capital "S" both deliberate and derisive, a holdover from what Orin thought of as his internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance—would complicate the sequence. Subjects had a tendency toward earnest, unbidden gestures: talking as though morning were a shared phenomenon, attempting to wrap him in the tangled warmth of their limbs, even cooking eggs with a kind of oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive. The worst was the silence, the gap in conversation where their gaze hung too long on him, expectant. Alone, though, wasn’t better. The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Meanwhile, Orin’s nocturnally tormented with disturbing nightmares, dreams of falling through endless black space from great heights, or being chased by human-sized spiders, or sometimes both, dreams of enormous spiders pursuing him to a rooftop’s edge, from which he awakes totally emotionally drained and suffocated and physically drenched in sweat. Orin’s constructed a number of morning rituals to mitigate the queasy, sucked-out feeling his dreams give him, which rituals have grown more repetitive and elongated with time, such that he now needs to drink multiple cups of coffee, have two or sometimes three showers, and go on a run before he feels even remotely normal. On those mornings when he has a Subject still in his bed from the night before, and therefore for obvious reasons can’t indulge his full routine, he finds himself privately ruminating on his disturbing and repetitive nightmares while he and the Subject are cuddling, chatting or cooking breakfast together, all while she remains totally oblivious to his tormented internal state. So that paradoxically, waking up next to a partner actually makes him feel even greater discomfort and alienation than if he were alone. Though make no mistake, mornings alone are almost unbearably oppressive, even the routines do little to alleviate Orin’s dread of the day ahead, the coming day seeming to him alternately like an insurmountable vertical climb or yet another fall from a great height.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: Though it took long reading excerpt 2 to really understand what was going on in this story, I still think excerpt  1 is better. Para 2 has some clunky sentences such as 'On those mornings when he has a Subject still in his bed from the night before, and therefore for obvious reasons can’t indulge his full routine' which feels overly long and poorly set-up. In this case, some of the shorter sentences of excerpt  1 help to maintain pace and fluidity such as 'Alone, though, wasn’t better', which gets to the point quickly, whist still feeling stylish and not just for function. This once is close as I got a bit more coherence from excerpt  2, but better fluidity from 1, which made it more effective, for me.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead. He walked on. Further on he came to a swamp that fell nightmarish on his eyes in all its nakedness of trees and dark figures dimly hominoid seemingly skulking in the mire. With a wary toe he tested the swampwater and reeled backwards at its unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation. He would not go this way. Retracing his steps back to the road and setting out upon it again he soon saw a man up ahead. The man tapped and swept a walking stick before him, feeling his way through that forever darkness only the blind knew the language of. The man smiled at Holme as he passed. Where the blind man was going Holme had already been, and Holme wondered then if anyone had informed the man of the grimness of what lay ahead at the end of the road. Walking on he lingered on what was not lost on him, the blind man’s incapability of seeing the burnt-out trees or even the road before him, not ever knowing where he’s going, but still following the road. No, he thought. He didn’t know where he was going.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. The charred and twisted trees rose up from the swampland like ancient mariners frozen in their death throes, their blackened limbs reaching toward a colorless sky that held neither sun nor promise. He tested the mire with one boot and watched the earth shudder and contract like something alive yet unborn, the surface dimpling and rising again in slow persistent waves that spoke of depths best left unplumbed. Through the dead forest came a sound like bones rattling, though there was nothing there but naked branches clicking together in a wind that seemed to carry voices. Then came the blind man, tapping his way along the road's edge with a stick worn smooth as glass, his face lifted in permanent expectation, smiling as if he knew some secret that the seeing world had lost. Holme watched him pass, this prophet of the wastes, and thought how the man's blindness might be a mercy in such a place as this. For what use were eyes in a world become nothing but ash and shadow, where even the trees had forgotten their own names and stood like sentinels at the gates of some darker realm that lay just beyond the next bend in the road, waiting with infinite patience for travelers who would never return.

It feels like a great story teller has weaved together just the right words to help truly grasp what exactly is happening. Excerpt 1 just feels like each sentence was given a very heavy period after each thought.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Further along he passed into a swamp made up of naked trees and other dimly hominoid forms that moved too slowly and caught their breath at each others' fingerlike edges. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The road lay before him, a trail of ash and dust, a ribbon unfurling through the skeletal remains of a forest.  Charred trees clawed at the sky, their branches like the limbs of the damned, twisted and broken.  The air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy on his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing.He ventured on, the road leading him into a swamp, a place where reality seemed to fray at the edges.  The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.

The inclusion of the blind man in the second excerpt felt more like a minor observation whereas it felt like it was the substance of excerpt 1. written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The road lay before him, a trail of ash and dust, a ribbon unfurling through the skeletal remains of a forest.  Charred trees clawed at the sky, their branches like the limbs of the damned, twisted and broken.  The air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy on his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing.He ventured on, the road leading him into a swamp, a place where reality seemed to fray at the edges.  The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Holme walked on. Holme wondered if the man sensed also the desolation around him or if someone had described it or directed him to the grim swamp to which he now headed. He thought of warning the blind man but did not. For in truth he thought there’s no better fate on the other end.

The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. "Take her with the others," he said, his voice flat as a snake's belly on hot pavement. Bobby Lee's face split in a yellow grin. "Some fun!" he said, but The Misfit's eyes had gone distant, like he was watching something terrible coming down the road toward them all. "It's no real pleasure in life," he said, and for a moment his face looked like it might crack open and show whatever darkness had been growing inside him since before he could remember. The sky above them was the exact color of a bruise, and somewhere in the distance a whip-poor-will called like it was mourning something that hadn't died yet.

For example, in describing The Misfit's thoughts on the existence of god, the writer closes the sentence and then starts a new sentence with, "The Misfit Wondered." Nonetheless, it is coherent, I think I can ascertain the story better from this excerpt. Excerpt 2 utilizes good metaphors to describe the emotions and actions of the characters, but it almost overuses them. Nonetheless, the story is more fluent and effective.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Standing on the yellow road in the bright sun, the grandmother before him and Hiram and Bobby Lee just behind, The Misfit sunk deeper into his bitter thinking. There can be no proof of anything—nothing earthly and nothing above—and certainly nothing like salvation for good deeds, or a father waiting and observing from some heavenly perch—and if there was no way to verify the existence of a real God, why live as if that God was watching? The Misfit wondered. The grandmother had on a hat with a brim that cast her face into aged shadows. Her mouth, a flat line, disturbed The Misfit and put a lump in his throat. But the grandmother’s face changed then, softened and clarified, and a beautiful smile spread from her to him. “You are one of my own children,” she said with great compassion, her voice loud and certain, outstretching feeble arms. The Misfit felt a wave of revulsion rising hot and tumorous in his chest and, recoiling, raised his gun and shot her three times. After, the grandmother’s body limp and lifeless in the ditch, the smile remained on her face. Even slumped, her hat upturned beside her, she had an air of perfect grace. Some question of forgiveness came then to The Misfit, which he carefully discarded and, taking off his glasses, surveyed her briefly with pale, defenseless eyes. “Get rid of her,” he told Hiram and Bobby Lee. “Put her with the others.” Bobby Lee chuckled, slapping Hiram on the shoulder, and said “Fun, real fun.” The Misfit turned cool eyes toward him, setting his jaw. “No, Bobby Lee,” he said, “it is not fun—not fun. There is no real pleasure in life.” He turned away from the body and walked on down the yellow road.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The Misfit stood there with his black hat tilted back on his head and his eyes gleaming like two wet stones in the gathering dusk. His face was all angles and shadows, the kind that spoke of something gone wrong in the blood generations back. The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. "Take her with the others," he said, his voice flat as a snake's belly on hot pavement. Bobby Lee's face split in a yellow grin. "Some fun!" he said, but The Misfit's eyes had gone distant, like he was watching something terrible coming down the road toward them all. "It's no real pleasure in life," he said, and for a moment his face looked like it might crack open and show whatever darkness had been growing inside him since before he could remember. The sky above them was the exact color of a bruise, and somewhere in the distance a whip-poor-will called like it was mourning something that hadn't died yet.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Misfit turned his head and looked the grandmother in her eyes. “Doesn’t it make you feel all raw to think about it?” he asked her. “That God may be real, but you can never know it? Not for sure?” The grandmother looked back at him, her face hard at first, then growing soft. She looked at Hiram, who spit into the road, and then at Bobby Lee, who rubbed his eyes with his dirty fingers. She looked back at The Misfit. “I can see why you might feel raw,” she said. “Yes, I can see that.” She pressed her lips together. “May I touch you?” she asked. Bobby Lee snapped his head around to look at her. The Misfit smiled. “Sure,” he said. The grandmother reached a cold and papery hand toward him and pressed her palm to his stubbled face. “My child,” she said. “You are my child.” She closed her eyes and laughed, and The Misfit took his gun out and shot her between her eyes, so that her nose was dashed away. She fell immediately backwards into the ditch and lay there, crumpled, her mouth mangled into a sort of smile. The Misfit took off his glasses and his eyes were pale and defenseless. “Get rid of her,” he said to Bobby Lee and Hiram. Bobby Lee chuckled. “What’s got you giggling like a little girl?” The Misfit snapped. “It’s just fun, is all,” said Bobby Lee. The Misfit turned and hit him, hard and quick across the face. Bobby Lee put a hand to his lip and frowned. He drew his hand away to find that his bottom lip was bleeding. “There is no real pleasure in life,” said The Misfit. “Now, pick her up and put her with the others so we can get rid of ‘em proper.”
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Misfit’s pale eyes, magnified by the thick lenses of his spectacles, seemed to devour her crumpled form.  His fingers traced the outline of her face, a grotesque caress that mirrored the distortion of his soul. He paused, a flicker of something unreadable in those magnified eyes. It might have been pity, but more likely it was the cold fascination of a child pulling wings off a fly. He observed her, this broken vessel of a woman, with the same clinical detachment he might have applied to a pinned insect, struggling vainly against its inevitable end. He was a collector of sorts. The Misfit rose, a specter in the twilight.  His glasses, now askew, reflected the dying light, casting a distorted glow on his gaunt features.He straightened them with a trembling hand, a gesture of futile order in a world spiraling into chaos.  “No real pleasure in life,” he repeated, the words a hollow mantra in the deepening silence.  The Misfit’s eyes, as he aimed the gun at the grandmother, held a chilling blend of detachment and desperation.  The gun’s retort shattered the stillness, a sound as hollow as the abyss that consumed him. The grandmother’s body slumped, a broken marionette in the roadside tableau.  The Misfit knelt, the gun dangling from his hand like a forgotten toy.  His fingers traced the outline of her face, a grotesque caress that mirrored the distortion of his soul.  The grandmother’s eyes flickered open, a spark of life in the encroaching darkness. You’re one of my own children,” she rasped, her voice a fragile echo in the desolate landscape.  The Misfit recoiled as if struck, a spasm of violence rippling through him.  The gun barked again, a final punctuation mark to her existence.Her body settled into the dust, a macabre parody of peace.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: There is more coherence and a natural flow to Excerpt1.  The characters are defined as the grandmother, the "misfit", Hiram and Bobby Lee.  The is more smoothness to the progression of this story in Excerpt1.  Excerpt1 has definitive beginning to end points so it is easier to comprehend the story as it is being told in Excerpt1.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: The grandmother’s face, shadowed by the wide brim of her hat, turned toward The Misfit, her trembling hand reaching as if to steady herself against the weight of her own words. Her voice, cracked and earnest, declared him as one of her own children, the statement hanging between them like a fragile thread in the stifling air. The Misfit’s pale eyes blinked behind thick glasses that reflected the distant sun, making him appear less man, more hollow instrument, tuned to discord. Hiram and Bobby Lee stood like rough-hewn statues, their hands idle but primed, their smirks a mockery of the tension thickening the moment. The grandmother’s outstretched hand shook with an urgency that seemed to belie her fragile clarity—a clarity forged by fear and sudden grace.Then came the shots, three in succession, each one punching the air with finality. Her body folded into the red clay ditch as if she were part of the earth all along, her hand still outstretched but now unyielding. A faint, enigmatic smile lingered on her lips, a puzzling counterpoint to the violence that had stilled her breath. The Misfit lowered his weapon slowly, his face twisted not in rage but something deeper—a silent rage turned inward, an unanswered question echoing in his marrow. He removed his glasses, wiped them carefully, and stared at the starkness of her lifeless form, his pale eyes vulnerable, almost raw.Bobby Lee chuckled, kicking a stone idly. “That was a fun one,” he said, his grin cruel. The Misfit turned his head sharply, his voice low and flinty. “She was closer to something than I’ll ever be,” he muttered, almost to himself. Then louder, with a bitter edge, “No pleasure in this life, none at all.” He spat into the dirt as they dragged her into the shadows.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: The Misfit looked at the old woman who had risen on to her knees in the damp grass and begun to pray. Hearing the familiar words made him lose his sense of urgency for it recalled to his mind the prayers he had memorized and repeated as a boy. The promise of redemption had appealed to him then but as a grown man he knew to trust only those things he could see for himself and verify firsthand. He would have given anything to have proof of his own everlasting soul or anyone else’s, but no sign had ever revealed itself to him and so the promises had turned curdled and turned bitter in his heart. The grandmother watched the Misfit’s face change as she prayed. She saw him illuminated and transformed into a young child, long before he was ever a killer, with a soul as pure and innocent as her son’s had once been. “You’re one of my own children!” she cried and reached out to him. But the sudden flicker of her outstretched white hand made the Misfit recoil and shoot. He shot three times in quick succession until she had crumpled and fallen back into the ditch. He stood over her in the ditch and watched her lips settle into a faint smile. He removed his wire-rimmed glasses and used his handkerchief to wipe the flecks of blood off them. Without the lenses his eyes were pale and defenseless and he let them pass over her lifeless body once before he replaced the frames and turned to Bobby Lee and Hiram. “Bury her with the others,” he said. “Boy, ain’t we havin’ some fun today?” Bobby Lee hooted, but the Misfit cut him off. “There’s no real pleasure in life,” he said sharply and walked back to the car.

The choice of words is also simpler and easy to comprehend making the flow seamless while reading. the tone fits the scene perfectly and the structure of the sentences is quiet okay.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: When Thomas Wolfe declared you can't go home again, he hadn't reckoned with the stubborn geography of the heart, that relentless compass that forever points to our beginning place. Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.

Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: I prefer excerpt 1, as the flow of this writing is clear, as opposed to 2, where there are too many lists. In 1, the writing is smooth and the ideas work well together, allowing the reader to 'see into the mind' of the writer. It draws upon the emotions of the writer, clearly conveying their thoughts.

Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Reason:
Excerpt 2 is a better work due to the fact that it presents ideas that flow more in a controlled and clear manner. It begins with a question that is well-known to people regarding home, organically introduces Thomas Wolfe, and then gradually gets down to the subject of the question, i.e., that home is not in physical buildings, but in childhood and perception. The development is deliberate and not wandering. Titles such as Home is in the sinew, in the flesh and it is the youthful perception serve to drive home the point without being overbearing.
Excerpt 1 has a lot of imagination and is usually too metaphorical. There is a stacking up of images--"dragons and dreams," "shadow-dance of memory," "song that keeps singing"-- to the extent that the emphasis is diluted and the emotional effectiveness is lost. The density and the fluency are present, but it seems to be overwritten.
Excerpt 2 is more successful at accomplishing the same objective because it tells a little less, gives more emphasis to rhythm and retrospection rather than overloading the text with imagery, and lets the concept of home as childhood just come clean and convincingly.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.

There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.

It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: excerpt  1 is easier to comprehend as its more clear statements that flow well together and effectively portray what the author is trying to convey about the childhood descriptions and emotions as excerpt 2 is usually words that is more poetic and for me does not flow well with the article.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: She’d said, “I want to handle this in my own way, on my own terms.”Her words hung in the air, heavy with finality and a hint of defiance.“I’m tired of waiting,” she continued, her voice a mix of weariness and determination.“I’m tired of this body failing me, of the endless treatments, the uncertainty.”She spoke of wanting to die peacefully, naturally, without any interference.“I don’t want any interventions, any disruptions,” she’d said.“I don’t want anyone trying to prolong this… existence.” She paused, a wry smile flickering across her face.“I don’t want anyone trying to play God,” she added, her tone a blend of humor and solemnity.Her words echoed in my mind as I walked down the street, the weight of our conversation pressing on me.I thought about her situation, her desire for autonomy, her frustration with the slow, unpredictable decay of her body.I thought about her wish for a peaceful, natural death, her refusal to let anyone “play God.”I thought about her insistence on secrecy, her plea for me not to mention her plans to anyone, not even my closest confidantes.I felt a knot of tension tighten in my chest, a conflict between my loyalty to her and my own need to process this heavy situation.I thought about the consequences of her choice, the potential legal ramifications, the emotional toll it would take on those who cared about her. I thought about my own role in this, my promise to support her, my fear of being implicated, my desire to protect her and myself.I felt a surge of guilt, a sense of betrayal, as I remembered the conversation I’d had with my therapist, the one person I’d confided in, breaking my promise to her.I tried to justify my actions, telling myself that I needed someone to talk to, someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield.But the guilt lingered, a constant reminder of my broken promise.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Excerpt one addresses the topic of patient autonomy much more clearly and in a much more palatable way than excerpt two. The statement "If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then?" does not even make sense to me. The two are very clearly written from different perspectives and overall the effectiveness, coherence and fluency are better in excerpt one.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly.
