written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt two is much more engaging and fluent than excerpt one. Excerpt one is a bit confusing in the way it is written. Specifically, the hypothetical questions said to the reader / self as one reads feels unnecessary. The second excerpt is much more 'adult' in it's style and is more fluent.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Jack stood there, fists balled in his jacket pockets, words tearing out of him like barbed wire through flesh. "Twenty years we been at this, En. Twenty goddamn years of sneakin up here like outlaws, like we done somethin wrong. You got me on this short leash, always yankin me back when I get too close to somethin real. Christ, I'm sick of it. Sick of these few days we grab like scraps under the table. You think I wanted this half-life? Living off memories of Brokeback till they're wore thin as old leather?" His voice cracked, raw as windburn. "I wish I knew how to quit you." The words hung between them like smoke in still air. Ennis swayed, color draining from his face like water from a broken cup, then his knees buckled and he went down hard on the packed dirt. "Jesus," Jack shouted, lunging forward, thinking heart attack, stroke, something busted loose inside that couldn't be fixed. But Ennis's shoulders were heaving, great gasping sobs tearing out of him, the kind that leave a man hollow. Jack stood frozen, watching his friend shake apart, knowing any touch might shatter what was left. When the storm passed, Ennis climbed to his feet, brushed dirt from his jeans like nothing had happened. They stood in the heavy silence, steam rising between them from their breath in the mountain air, neither looking at the other. Nothing changed. Nothing could change. The moment passed like so many before it, settling into the collection of hurts they carried, weight added to weight until the burden seemed natural as breathing.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. I’m like your dog, chokin on your short leash. All I want is to…it doesn’t matter, do it? Imma dog frothin at the end of your fuckin leash. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Jack leaned against the post, his chest heaving, words spilling out in a torrent, raw as the gouged earth beneath his boots. “I can’t do this anymore, Ennis. It ain’t just the damn mountain. You hold me like I’m some stray dog on a leash, pullin’ me close when you want and kickin’ me away when you don’t. Ain’t a life, this. Not for me.” His voice cracked, ricocheted into the dry air. “Wish I knew how to quit you, but it’s like tryin’ to wrench a fishhook outta your own throat.” He tipped his hat back, his eyes watery but fierce, daring the other man to respond. Ennis stood frozen, fists tight, the sinews of his neck stretched taut like old barbed wire. When the words hit their mark, it was like a shot fired too close—he crumpled, knees buckling, gasping for air as though Jack’s truths had knocked it clean out of him. “Jesus,” Jack muttered, rushing forward, unsure if he should steady Ennis or step away. The distance between them felt insurmountable, a chasm carved out of years of furtive touches and unspoken words. For a moment, there was only the rasp of their breath, mingling with the faint hum of crickets and the whisper of dry grass. Ennis lifted his head, the shadows on his face deep, his expression unreadable. He staggered to his feet, brushing off Jack’s hand, and the weight of their shared silence pressed in. Nothing was mended, no path forward uncovered. Just the same cycle of longing and restraint, heartbreak hanging in the air like steam from a kettle left too long on the flame, inevitable and unyielding, rising but never dispersing.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Both excerpt s are compelling but I prefer the introduction of excerpt 2, it sets the scene and you become immersed in the scene from the start. I like the use of onomatopoeia like 'cracked' and 'gasping', it all feels very visceral. Excerpt 1 possibly has too much dialogue so it's harder to follow what it going on.

written_by_MFA024.Excerpt1: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: Kant's coming out email sat in his drafts folder like a grenade with the pin half-pulled, while he spent weeks A/B testing subject lines, as if the right combination of words could defuse three decades of queerness into something digestible for his mother's WeChat circles. He'd crafted seventeen versions, each more baroque than the last, padding them with disclaimers and preemptive responses to imagined objections, until the final draft read like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation. The responses, when they finally came, were an anticlimactic parade of heart emojis and "love you no matter what"s—the kind of tepid acceptance that made him wonder if perhaps he wasn't gay enough to warrant proper drama. His coworkers replied with the practiced neutrality of people who'd attended exactly one diversity training, while his mother's response ("Ok. Did you eat dinner?") felt like being handed a participation trophy for surviving thirty-one years of internal torment. He'd prepared for scorched earth but got lukewarm validation, and now here he was, somehow lonelier in his freedom, spending his newly authentic life watching YouTube compilations of gay wedding flash mobs and ordering rainbow-colored socks he'd never wear. The Year of Damp Feet, he called it in his journal, though he knew the phrase would sound better in someone else's memoir. His therapist called this "adjustment period" progress, but it felt more like trading one closet for another—this one just happened to have better lighting and an Amazon Prime subscription. The truth was, he'd gotten good at being afraid, had built his personality around it like a pearl around grit, and now that the fear was gone, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he'd peaked at being closeted, that he'd somehow gentrified his own identity into something too palatable to matter, too sanitized for the revolution he'd imagined himself starring in.
written_by_MFA024.Reason: Its an engaging piece. it uses figurative language, precise word of choice and has the ability to engage in emotional states thus making it superior in terms of coherence , fluency and effectiveness.  Excerpt 2 explores a more complex emotional landscape, moving beyond simple disappointment to a feeling of being somehow lonelier in his freedom and questioning if he "peaked at being closeted."

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Kant, a connoisseur of solitude, had always envisioned his coming-out as a cataclysmic event, a meteor strike that would leave a crater in his life.  He'd spent weeks crafting the perfect email, a digital dove carrying the olive branch of his truth.  His imagination, a master of disaster, painted vivid scenes of his mother's tearful rejection, his friends recoiling in horror, and his colleagues whispering behind his back.But reality, it turned out, was a terrible painter.  The email launched, and instead of a meteor shower, there was a gentle rain of heart emojis from friends, muted acknowledgments from coworkers, and a carefully worded acceptance from his parents.  No drama, no disinheritance, not even a decent argument. Kant was baffled.  Where was the transformative growth?  The epic struggle he had envisioned himself overcoming?  Instead of relief, he felt a perverse disappointment, a sense of anticlimax that left him feeling strangely unfulfilled.His post-coming-out life was marked by inertia, an endless parade of solitary evenings and damp socks.  He'd walk home alone, his footsteps echoing in the cavernous silence of his apartment, the air thick with the scent of unwashed laundry and existential loneliness.He'd spend hours on the internet, scrolling through endless feeds of other people's curated lives, each post a tiny dagger to his heart.  He'd watch reality TV, the inane chatter of the contestants a poor substitute for human connection. He'd even tried dating, but his heart wasn't in it.  Each date felt like a performance, a carefully choreographed dance of small talk and forced smiles.  He'd find himself longing for the solitude of his apartment, the comforting embrace of his damp socks. Kant's year of damp feet was a testament to the enduring power of fear, a fear that had not only kept him closeted for years but had also robbed him of the joy of his own liberation.  He was free, but he was alone, a prisoner of his own making.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: For seven months, thirty-one-year old Kant tried to come out. He had decided that the most optimized method would take the form of mass email, as text could be perfected, and, in these many months, perfected the text: it was nearly a work of art, forthcoming without oversharing (he’d received feedback from internet forums), and grammar checked. It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. By the time that he’d finished the anxious rigamarole, a few replies had come in, and the reality became obvious: he’d been received with open-arms and heart emojis. His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. In the days after he’d sent the email, he didn’t feel compelled to download any apps or sit at a stool in the gay bar down the street. A part of him wished for adversity, or at least the accompanying opportunity to rise above it, but he was left with an understanding that nothing had changed, that declaration didn’t always inspire action. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.

His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Kant, a connoisseur of solitude, had always envisioned his coming-out as a cataclysmic event, a meteor strike that would leave a crater in his life.  He'd spent weeks crafting the perfect email, a digital dove carrying the olive branch of his truth.  His imagination, a master of disaster, painted vivid scenes of his mother's tearful rejection, his friends recoiling in horror, and his colleagues whispering behind his back.But reality, it turned out, was a terrible painter.  The email launched, and instead of a meteor shower, there was a gentle rain of heart emojis from friends, muted acknowledgments from coworkers, and a carefully worded acceptance from his parents. Instead of relief, he felt a perverse disappointment, a sense of anticlimax that left him feeling strangely unfulfilled.His post-coming-out life was marked by inertia, an endless parade of solitary evenings and damp socks. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Kant spent hours drafting the email, toggling between subject lines (“A Word to Everyone,” “FYI,” and, finally, “Coming Out”) like they were tarot cards predicting his fate. In his head, each recipient’s reaction unspooled in unrelenting technicolor: his mother, weeping silently in the kitchen as she diced onions for the biryani she thought would fix his mood; his old college roommate forwarding the email to their group chat with the caption, “Knew it”; his boss, furrowing his brow at the computer, typing, “Not sure why this concerns me professionally.” These imagined catastrophes paraded through his thoughts as he clicked send, his trembling hand a cheap metaphor for the fear wedged in his sternum. Then: nothing. The world didn’t combust. Instead, his notifications flooded with low-stakes affirmations—heart emojis from friends, a “proud of you, dude” text from a cousin, even a begrudging “love you” from his father, which Kant suspected had been typed under duress from his mother. He should’ve felt relief, triumph even, but instead, there was this sneaking, hollow ache. He’d braced himself for rejection, a narrative arc with stakes, but life handed him a shrug and a pat on the back. What was the point of all that dread if no one made it cinematic? The next few weeks stretched out like an overcooked spaghetti noodle—soft, limp, no bite. Without the anticipated martyrdom, Kant drifted into what he called his “Year of Damp Feet,” shuffling around his apartment in unwashed socks, ignoring texts inviting him to “finally celebrate.” He scrolled through his inbox, rereading replies, hoping to stumble on something more… dramatic. Wasn’t this supposed to be the pivot point of his life? Instead, he remained unchanged, realizing that even monumental self-revelations couldn’t save him from the everyday inertia of being Kant. A hero’s journey, sure—but with no villain, no fight, just the lukewarm end credits rolling over silence.

written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 2 is my selection for a couple of particular reasons. Excerpt 1 might be straight forward and easily understandable. Both are easy to understand from the coherence perspective, but excerpt 1 meanders and bounces around to different thoughts from sentence to sentence whereas excerpt 2 provides us with a pretty straight forward narrative that is easy to follow. Coherent writing should be showing us the narrative through it's imagery and sensory language which is why excerpt two alternates between what Kant is physically doing versus how he envisions the immediate reactions around him. This is also what makes it score points in the fluency category as it flows smoothly bouncing between inner monologue and action that moves the plot forward easily. From reading both excerpts, it felt like the effect the author was trying to convey was Kant tragically envisioning that his coming out would be a transformational moment that solidified his identity and gave him a sense of peace. However, the boring everyday reaction he gets from it reminds him coldly that coming out did not solve all of his problems. When you look at both excerpts, 2 is more effective at both showing us this happening and giving us a sense of the immediate blow to the ego the action has on Kant which wraps up nicely in sad, self-reflective ending.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Mrs. Dalloway, stepping out into the June morning, thought how she would fetch the flowers herself, for Lucy had quite enough to manage with those men from Rumpelmayer's coming. The fresh air caught her face (how young she felt, how perpetually astonished!) and sent her mind spinning back to Bourton, to those mornings when she was eighteen, when she would burst out onto the terrace and feel the world pause, crystalize, become both solemn and effervescent in that early hour. Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! Such a thing to remember as clearly as if their breakfast was shared only yesterday, when in fact yesterday Clarissa had been deciding about the flowers, deciding to buy them from the yellow and blue shop she now rapidly approaches, with the vibrant window displays; the freshest flowers, she knew, those with the richest and most enduring smell, must come from this shop, and now she would buy them herself.

Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! Such a thing to remember as clearly as if their breakfast was shared only yesterday, when in fact yesterday Clarissa had been deciding about the flowers, deciding to buy them from the yellow and blue shop she now rapidly approaches, with the vibrant window displays; the freshest flowers, she knew, those with the richest and most enduring smell, must come from this shop, and now she would buy them herself.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Clarissa Dalloway, a woman of exquisite sensibility, stepped out into the vibrant London morning. She had decided to buy the flowers herself, a small act of consideration for Lucy, her servant, who was already bustling about with the preparations for the evening's gathering. The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.

The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.
written_by_MFA004.Reason: Fluency is better in this excerpt as there are no grammar errors e.g. "doctor's" in excerpt 2. This is also the case for the characters in the excerpt, they are presented well and the reader knows who they are instantly. Excerpt 2 feels more disjointed and the ideas are not flowing together well.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Excerpt 2 is trying too hard with the convoluted sentences and attempts at interesting word choice. It makes it harder work to read without really adding anything - the result is rather lumpen and lifeless. Excerpt 1 expresses it thoughts much more cohesively, clearly and effectively, although it also has some slightly silly choice of language - is 'mild lacrimal event' supposed to be satire?

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens. I resolve to become the kind of artist who can transform bad forms of collectivity—bedbugs, or the crowds now surging toward Times Square—into glimpses of their potential for a kind of unity, a communal body. written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.

From all of this comes focus and comprehension, with a determination to be ok. 

Excerpt one feels a little dystopian, like she's drowning but has come to terms with it: '...with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together...' They both end on a positive note, objectively, while excerpt one is full of melancholy and desperation, but excerpt two is hopeful and accepting of everything that's happened and will happen. 

On a random note, it feels as though it's very windy wherever she is, and dark.

There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. The Hudson River, the Palisades on the other side, even the movement of the clouds, fail to trigger the same response.I breathe deeply, trying to identify the chemical compounds in the air.  I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. Who could have predicted that from our community of intellectuals and worriers, of boys who measured their worth by the heft of their Hebrew school books and the precision of their bar mitzvah portions, would emerge this specimen of Nordic perfection? The Swede, with his impossible blue eyes and hair the color of straw, who moved across the athletic field like some magnificent shiksa fantasy come to life, became our collective dream of transformation. Here was a Jewish boy who could smash through defensive lines on the football field with the force of a Gentile, who could arc a basketball through the hoop with gymnastic grace, who could swing a baseball bat as if it were his birthright rather than something we'd borrowed from the other America. And how we needed him then, needed to believe in this anomaly, this statistical impossibility of nature who happened to daven at our synagogue! While our mothers whispered anxiously about cousins in Europe and our fathers scanned casualty lists in the Newark News with trembling hands, The Swede was our ticket to invincibility, our pass into that other realm where Jewish boys didn't have to be smart because they were beautiful, didn't have to be crafty because they were strong. We projected onto him all our desperate hopes of acceptance, of transcendence – this boy who looked like he'd stepped out of a Nazi propaganda poster but wore a chai around his neck and could recite his Haftorah portion without a single mistake. The Swede was our temporary escape from who we were, from what we feared, from the relentless drumbeat of war news that threatened to drown out even the sound of our prayers.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I was a boy of World War II and a boy of Newark. The war was far away and beyond my understanding, but the dread and threat of it spilled across the ocean and flooded every home in my city. Lots of our men were off fighting, and lots of them would never come home. Rations of oil and sugar were dispensed through clenched fists. We spent many nights huddled around the radio and forgetting to breathe. It was a time of need, which is—according to the comic books—the perfect time for a hero to arrive. Newark’s wartime hero was a high school boy named Seymour Irving Levov, who we nicknamed “The Swede” because of his blond hair and blue eyes. He was a paragon of greatness in my neighborhood, and his athletic ability was the stuff of legend; regardless of the sport he played, he always clinched the win for his team. The Swede’s consistent excellence in football, basketball, and baseball gave my community something to rally for. Being Jewish, most of us tended to prioritize academic achievements over physical feats, but the Swede changed things. We’d turn up to his games with homemade banners and clumsily invented cheers, among them “S-W-E-D-E, get this team to victory!” Watching the force of his kick, the graceful arch of his throw, and the shattering power of his swing shrouded us in a feeling of awe that was rarely experienced outside of Temple. When the Swede was on the field or on the court, my whole neighborhood was in the palm of his hand. He had unwittingly become a symbol of invincibility, of innocence, of hope that the terrible war would leave us unscathed, passed over like we had smeared lamb blood on our doors. Looking back, I don’t know if our hero arrived or if our hero was created, but the Swede was more than willing to shoulder the burden.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: This one was difficult to choose because I think both are really well written. I chose Excerpt 1 though because I think it provided a setup about why The Swede was needed for their community, more than Excerpt 2 did. The descriptions in Excerpt 1 were more visceral and spoke to me more.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.

The writing flows like a story and keeps me as the reader interested. It explains his impact clearly without being too wordy or jumping around too much.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better because it reads like a good book and you can imagine the story in your mind. The second excerpt is worse because it reads more like the story happening all at once and is too confusing to follow along. Excerpt 1 flows wells and is fluent is telling a story.
