written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Reading this statement is very simple because it makes you feel the natural tone of the statement, and also it makes the statement very complete. In this regard, choosing excerpt 2 over 1 makes a lot of meaning because you can feel the naturalness of the statement in a whole.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Both excerpt s are good, but Excerpt 1 is more real and focuses on the woman instead of the mistress. I like the phrases "brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life" and "polyester pantsuit-ness of it all." Both are very descriptive and vivid when describing the story.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt one is the better one in my opinion. It wove the story together well. The second story was too blunt and not very coherent. I think that the first one showed a good creative writing ability while the second just seemed like the writer was getting it over with.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I stumbled into the job because I heard about it from the local drunk. The local drunk had uneven stubble and a feminine watery quality around his eyes. It was seasonal, but I was fine with that. I never liked to stay in the same job too long. It was free and it was simple, and I don’t know of a man who doesn’t value those things above all else. It was a small amount of work compared to most jobs, monotonous, sure, but I could think about other things, like girls or what I wanted to eat. Some people didn’t, but I always liked to work around Christmastime. It was only my second day when I met the big woman. She had a mole over the left side of her lip shaped like a heart. She had short hair, and her breasts were small for how big she was. Her eyes were thin and suspicious. She opened the door when I came to put her mail in the box. She wore a white, lace robe that was meant for a smaller woman, and it made her hips look nice and round. She was smoking a cigarette delicately like a movie star, and she asked me to give her the mail. I did, three letters, and somehow we ended up talking, and I found out her husband was stationed somewhere in California. “It’s sorta dark, the loneliness,” she said, and I agreed with her. “You’re alone?” she asked. “No,” I said. “But you’re still lonely.” I shrugged and looked right at the sun. We organized it so we’d meet that night, at her house. It was her idea, but I didn’t exactly turn it down. I went over there after dinner and it was nice enough. We fooled around on her couch and I was pleasantly surprised by how good her figure was. She wasn’t all lumpy and stretched like big women can be. It went on like that for a couple nights, but by the third I was tired of it and that was the end of that. It was a good experience, all in all, and reminded me why I liked that job so much.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I drove down the street with a bag of letters slung over my shoulder like some half-assed Santa Claus in a postal uniform. Got the job from some drunk at the bar who said they were desperate for Christmas help, didn't even check my record. Perfect setup - walk around all day, drop paper in boxes, nobody breathing down your neck about quotas or time cards. Second day in, I'm working this neighborhood of tired houses with paint peeling off like dead skin when I see her. Big woman, not the Hollywood type, more like a female wrestler gone soft. She was watering dead flowers, her dress pulled tight across her ass, and when she bent over I nearly dropped the whole damn bag. "You the new mailman?" she asked, straightening up. I nodded, handed her some circulars and bills. She told me her husband was stationed in Germany, hadn't touched her in 8 months. Christ, the way she said it made my balls ache. I had a woman at home but she was always bitching about the rent, about my drinking, about everything. This one just wanted company. "Come by tonight," she said, giving me her address. I showed up at 9, half-drunk on cheap wine. The house smelled like potpourri and desperation. We didn't waste time talking - she led me straight to the bedroom, peeling off that housedress like a snake shedding its skin. For three days I'd deliver her mail, then deliver something else at night. But like everything else, it got old fast. The smell of her perfume started making me sick, her neediness felt like a noose. By the fourth day I was taking different routes, ducking behind hedges when I saw her watering those dead flowers. Looking back, being a mailman wasn't half bad - good hours, easy work, and lonely housewives with too much time on their hands. Hell, you didn't even have to try - they were so desperate they'd fuck anything in a uniform. Sometimes the best jobs are the ones that give you just enough money to drink and just enough time to fuck.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. A local drunk had mentioned they needed Christmas help at the post office, and that was enough for me. Walk around, dump letters in boxes, pretend to care. Not bad. My second day, I met her—big woman, bigger than me, with those arms that looked like they’d been lifting more than just grocery bags. She stood at the door like she’d been waiting for me all day. “Cold out,” she said, her breath heavy, warm, sweet and rotten at the same time. “Yeah,” I said, “but I don’t mind.” I minded, but I wasn’t about to tell her that. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. The place was warm, smelled like burned toast and old carpet. She poured me whiskey instead of coffee, and that was better. We moved from the kitchen to the couch to the bedroom like it was something we’d done before. A few days passed like that. But the thing about loneliness is, it doesn’t go away just because you put your hands on someone. Eventually, the whiskey bottle emptied, the room started feeling smaller, and her laugh turned into something I didn’t want to hear. The job was still there, but the excitement was gone. So I delivered the mail, took my paycheck, and let her find another man to fill the spaces her husband left behind. Being a mailman wasn’t bad. Good work if you like walking. Better work if you don’t mind a little company along the way.

Five days later I found her to be so one-note that I split. Besides, even when we were together, we were both still alone. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. My second day, I met her—big woman, bigger than me, with those arms that looked like they’d been lifting more than just grocery bags. She stood at the door like she’d been waiting for me all day. “Cold out,” she said, her breath heavy, warm, sweet and rotten at the same time. “Yeah,” I said, “but I don’t mind.” I minded, but I wasn’t about to tell her that. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. The place was warm, smelled like burned toast and old carpet. She poured me whiskey instead of coffee, and that was better. We moved from the kitchen to the couch to the bedroom like it was something we’d done before. A few days passed like that. Better work if you don’t mind a little company along the way.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. A young doctor in a white coat pressed against the back wall, studying a clipboard, while two nurses whispered near the buttons, their voices barely audible above the mechanical hum. The speakers crackled: "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to Ward 3." I watched the numbers illuminate one by one: three, four, five. The bag I had made was perfect—every stitch aligned with precision, the leather supple and warm like living skin. I had spent weeks crafting it, imagining her face when she would first hold it, how her fingers would trace the seams I had sewn with such care. Now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose, like the shears tucked carefully in my coat pocket. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt one has an unnatural flow. It keeps repeating the name: 'Dr Y from Respiratory Medicine' which interrupts your train of thought and makes the story harder to follow. I don't like the conversation held with himself in the middle of the excerpt as it just seems self-indulgent and unrealistic. The ending is too graphic which makes it seem weird. I much prefer excerpt 2 as it doesn't try to do too much. It tells the story in a natural, fluid way. Presenting one idea and then the next. It introduces the bag and that it might contain something important in a gentle way - at the start it says: 'I clutched the bag closer to my chest,' 'now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose'. I like this descriptive writing. It seems believable and you want to find out more. The description of her perceived thoughts on the bag are relevant and realistic. I like the use of metaphors to describe her heart. The ended is not too graphic but tells you enough so that the plot is effective.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The elevator hummed its ascent , its metallic echo chamber filled with the rustling of starched white coats and the hushed murmurs of worried voices.  Doctors and nurses, their footsteps brisk and purposeful, pressed against me, their faces etched with lines of clinical concern.  A woman, her hand clutching a crumpled tissue, sobbed softly in the corner, her body trembling with a grief I could not touch.  The tinny voice of the intercom announced, "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine," its monotone a stark contrast to the silent anxieties swirling within the elevator's steel box.I stood amidst this symphony of human emotion, my heart a steady drumbeat against my ribs, my purpose clear.  I was going to see her, the woman who had entrusted me with her memories, her fears, her hopes, woven into the very fabric of the bag I had crafted for her.  I would smile, offer gentle words, tell her how the bag, her bag, was a masterpiece, a testament to her strength, her resilience.  I would ask her to try it on, to feel the weight of it, the way it settled against her, a perfect fit. And then, as her eyes lit up with a flicker of trust, a spark of recognition, I would watch her heart, that fragile vessel of memory, beat against her chest, a tiny bird trapped within a cage of ribs.  I would slice the shears through her skin and cut her heart out. I'd hold her heart in my hands, its warmth a perverse comfort, its rhythm a dark symphony. And then, I'd claim the bag, mine alone, its rightful place by my side, its true purpose fulfilled.The elevator lurched to a halt.The shears lay nestled in my pocket, their sharp blades whispering promises of possession, of a bond that would be mine alone.It was the the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: I approach the hospital elevator. It is almost full up with nurses, doctors, and their patients. I slip myself between the heat of their bodies, which are all dressed in blue gowns or white coats. I press the button six. A voice comes on over a speaker hidden somewhere up above. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” the voice says. It repeats the words as the elevator whirs into motion and begins to rise. I wonder where in the building Dr. Y could be. I look down at the bag in my hands, admiring my fine craftsmanship–the softness of the leather, the straight, simple lines of my stitches. I have made it for the woman exactly to her specifications. It is undeniable. “Look,” I will say. “Look what I have made for you. See how beautiful it is?” I will offer it to her to try on. She will be grateful, of course, and in awe of the beauty of my hard work. She will try it on, adjusting the straps to her liking. She will arrange it this way and that: cross-body, or dangling from her fingers, or slung carelessly off the shoulder. “Do you trust me again?” I will ask. In the face of the beauty of the bag, she will have no choice but to say yes, to be nothing but thankful. And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim. My grip tightens on the sheers that I keep tucked behind the bag. The blades are long and sharp. They are a silver so bright that it flashes in the glare of the overhead elevator lighting when I sneak a look down at them. The elevator dings; we have arrived at the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Response 2 seems to be very vivid and makes a lot of sense, in the sense that you can easily and freely follow the story with the hope that you will get the full understanding. The choice of words used are very simple, and they make a lot of meaningful statements.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still. The voice over the intercom announced, “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to ward three,” in a steady monotone, a voice unbothered by the frantic shuffle of nurses and patients around me. The air was tinged with a faint medicinal scent, sharp and sterile, as though the building itself exhaled nothing but clean, cold breath. My thoughts drifted toward her, lying somewhere beyond these walls, fragile and unguarded.The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand. I imagined the look in her eyes as I approached, a flicker of recognition perhaps, then the inevitable softening—a crack in the shield of suspicion she might have built around herself. My words were carefully chosen in advance, rehearsed in the quiet moments of the previous night: admiration for her grace, a humble explanation of my creation, a plea for forgiveness wrapped in layers of calm sincerity.And yet, the weight of the shears burned against the lining of the bag, a cold promise of something darker. The thought of her chest rising and falling, her heart pulsing rhythmically beneath the soft fabric of her gown, stirred a sensation I couldn’t quite place. My grip on the strap tightened as the fantasy took shape—a vision of my hands steady, precise, separating her from the fragile organ that held her life. The bag would hold it perfectly, as it was meant to.The elevator dinged, and the doors slid open to reveal the sixth floor. The hall stretched out before me, fluorescent lights reflecting off the polished floors. I stepped out, the bag heavy in my hand, and began walking toward her room.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.

If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.

If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet. I really didn't. I just stood there with this goofy grin on my face - I probably looked like a complete madman - watching my kid sister in her blue coat having the time of her life. That killed me. It really did. My hunting hat was getting soaked but I didn't care about that either. It's funny, sometimes the things that make you the happiest are the things that get you all sopping wet and probably looking like a complete moron to everybody else. But that's the thing about happiness - it doesn't give a damn what you look like.Now I'm stuck in this crumby place, this rest home or whatever the hell you want to call it, and this hotshot psychoanalyst keeps asking me all these stupid questions about what I'm gonna do with my future. Like if I'm gonna "apply myself" when I go back to school. Jesus Christ, that kills me. These people and their goddam questions. Even old D.B. - he's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still can't help himself. He came to visit me yesterday with this English actress who was sort of beautiful in this fake, Hollywood way. As soon as she went to the bathroom - girls are always going to the bathroom when you're in the middle of something - D.B. starts in with the questions about everything I've been telling him. All about what happened and what I think about it now and all.The funny part is, the more I talk about all this stuff, the more I keep thinking about everybody. Even the people I didn't particularly like, for Chrissake. Like old Stradlater with his secret slob tendencies and Ackley with his pimples and Maurice. I keep thinking about them and missing them, in this crazy way. I don't even know why. I mean, they were all phonies in their own way, but I miss them anyway. That's the thing that drives me crazy in here - how you can hate somebody's guts one minute and then start missing them like hell the next. It's really ironical as hell. Sometimes I think maybe that psychoanalyst isn't so dumb after all, but I'd rather get kicked in the teeth than admit that to him. He'll probably ask me about my violent tendencies next time I see him. That's the trouble with psychoanalysts - they always want to know what everything means, even when things don't mean anything at all.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.

Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
written_by_MFA025.Reason:
I feel like these are both in the style of Catcher in the Rye (and perhaps Excerpt 2 is a section of it, or at least feels more like it's in keeping with what I remember of the original).

Excerpt 2 works better for me as it drops you straight into the stream of consciousness and it's apparent where the boundary is between the memory of Phoebe and the character's current situation, in the rest home. This helps in terms of not being distracted by how it's achieving understanding.

written_by_MFA025.Reason: I recognize this scene from Catcher in the Rye which I remember reading in high school. I cannot confirm if either are the original passage, but excerpt 2 really calls to mind the character of Holden Caulfield to me. One of the most provocative and effective things about excerpt 2 is how realistic and characterizing the language is. Describing a torrential downpour as "the way it does when you don't have a goddam umbrella" immediately feels like a conversational and relatable idea. I would argue that this is what makes the novel flow so well. You are invited to "experience" Holden in an authentic way that he shows through the way he communicates, which makes this novel such an easy and coherent read. Hearing someone talk is the most naturalistic way to absorb information, and the coherence of excerpt 2 flows like human language while also giving us the background of what's happening. This is also what makes it natural and smooth, such as how he demonstrates how he's feeling by saying "You think it'll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you're carrying this big stupid ache." Coherence and fluency come across pretty easy in a naturalistic dialogue style but the effectiveness of getting to experience Holden's voice is why this novel is so great.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
written_by_MFA002.Reason: Excerpt 2 sounds more like it is a college essay. There is something too formulaic and constructed about the way it is telling its story. The first excerpt feels like a conversation being had, or something far more personable than the second one does. It just flows more naturally despite being a shorter excerpt.

Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
