written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The Black Panther Party, a whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury, had been my crucible. I'd joined partly to prove a point, to silence the whispers that trailed me like a shadow. "Not Black enough," they hissed, both Black and white voices mingling in a chorus of disapproval. My crime? Muttering "Egads" during a heated basketball game, perhaps. Or maybe it was my novels, those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus, drawing accusations of elitism and worse, cultural betrayal. One particularly scathing review declared, "His Aeschylus is a betrayal of his Black heritage, a misguided attempt to elevate himself above his roots." The New York literary party, a swirling vortex of ambition and pretense, was no different. A literary agent, her eyes scanning the room for the next big thing, dismissed my work with a wave of her hand. "Forget Aeschylus," she scoffed, "write true, gritty real stories of Black life. That's what sells." I wanted to retort, "My life, my experience, isn't that Black enough for you?" But the words caught in my throat, choked by the weight of expectation. The agent, sensing my hesitation, moved on, her attention snagged by a performance artist reciting a monologue about the Black experience. The irony was thick enough to cut with a knife.  Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: I enjoyed reading excerpt 1 more. The writing style is more captivating and immediate, I think because of the use of quotations from different characters. The use of rhetorical questions is effective. Excerpt 2 feels less stylish, less accomplished, though it was still enjoyable to read. Both are fluent and coherent but excerpt 1 is especially effective.

Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The pain exploded in Wendy's side like a grenade of glass shards as she clawed her way up the stairs, each step a new universe of agony. Behind her—too close, Christ, too close—came the whisper-thump of Jack's feet, a sound she'd once found comforting during their late-night kitchen raids but now sent ice-water terror coursing through her veins. His laughter floated up, thick and wet with blood, a madman's carousel music. "Honey, come back! I just want to bash your brains in!" The roque mallet whooshed through the air, stirring her hair like a lover's caress. She reached the top landing, lungs burning, heart thundering against her ribs like it wanted to escape her chest—and why shouldn't it? Getting away seemed like the only sane response to this nightmare. That's when the door to her left burst open and a figure lurched out, wearing a moldering green ghoul mask that might've been funny at some teenage Halloween party twenty years ago. "GREAT PARTY, ISN'T IT?" it screamed, blowing a party favor that unrolled with a wet, obscene sound. Then it was gone, door slamming with such force it shook dust from the ceiling. Wendy's legs betrayed her and she went down hard, the carpet beneath her fingers writhing like living things—thousands of insects fleeing from the violence above. The elevator hummed to life somewhere in the bowels of the hotel, its ancient gears grinding like arthritic teeth. She tried to push herself up, but her side shrieked in protest. Jack's shadow loomed over her, distorted and massive on the wall. The mallet swung down in a silver arc of death, missing her by inches as Jack stumbled, his momentum carrying him forward. He crashed face-first into the carpet, blood spraying from his mouth in a fine crimson mist. But Wendy knew he wouldn't stay down long. In the Overlook Hotel, nothing stayed dead for long.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Wendy looked back and wished she hadn’t. Jack had a malevolent smile on his face, and blood dripped from his open mouth down his chin like fruit juice. He swung a roque mallet steadily from side to side as he advanced up the staircase toward her. “C’mere, Wendy,” he said, “or I’ll paint this wall with your pretty, pink little brains.” Wendy turned back around and willed herself to keep going up the staircase. Her side was electric with pain, but she grit her teeth and kept going until she was in the corridor, where she broke into a run. She was almost at the end when a large figure jumped out in front of her. “You’ve gotta come to the party!” he shouted. He wore a green mask with hideously contorted plastic features. “Party favor?” he said, and jammed a little box toward her. She darted around him and continued down the hall, running faster this time. A door slammed violently behind her, and she turned to see that the man had disappeared.The pain in her side was becoming so severe that, when she took her next step forward, she collapsed under the agony of it. She tried to contain her scream, but it came roaring out of her anyway. She balled her hands into fists and pounded them into the carpet, which appeared to move beneath her, the patterns snakelike and fluid.The elevator made an ominous noise as it crept up the shaft, and she got on her knees, gripping the wall to try and stand. The elevator doors peeled open, revealing Jack with his heavy mallet. He spotted her and smiled. “Those pretty brains,” he said, and staggered in her direction. She began to run again, and he was behind her quickly. She felt the whoosh of the mallet, the air from its force grazing the back of her neck. She ducked away, and watched as Jack’s momentum sent him tumbling face-down onto the carpet, blood scattering like gory diamonds. She continued down the hall without looking back, her gasps so loud they blocked out all other sound.

A door slammed violently behind her, and she turned to see that the man had disappeared.The pain in her side was becoming so severe that, when she took her next step forward, she collapsed under the agony of it. She tried to contain her scream, but it came roaring out of her anyway. She balled her hands into fists and pounded them into the carpet, which appeared to move beneath her, the patterns snakelike and fluid.The elevator made an ominous noise as it crept up the shaft, and she got on her knees, gripping the wall to try and stand. She ducked away, and watched as Jack’s momentum sent him tumbling face-down onto the carpet, blood scattering like gory diamonds. She continued down the hall without looking back, her gasps so loud they blocked out all other sound.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: Wendy gasped as she stumbled up the stairs, holding onto the railing with one hand. Each step sent a sharp pain through her side. She would’ve liked nothing better than to take a short rest but Jack’s voice behind her kept her going. “Wendy,” he slurred, grinning through bloody teeth, “come back here, sweetheart, so I can crush your bones like garlic cloves, what do you say?” She imagined feeling a gust of wind from the swing of Jack’s mallet behind her. At least the thundering of her pulse dulled the pain in her side. She turned corner after corner. Her feet barely touched the steps. The stairs seemed to stretch on endlessly. Finally, she reached the landing. She thought she had a second to breathe, when suddenly, a man—or something similar to a man— burst from a door. He wore a green ghoul mask and his suit reeked of mildew. Blowing a party favor that flapped in the air like a severed tongue, he shrieked, “Party time!” Wendy screamed and not knowing where else to go, stumbled backwards. The man vanished as abruptly as he’d appeared, slamming the door behind him. Wendy’s chest heaved. She collapsed to the floor. Her eyes felt heavy, but she told herself to stay awake, to just stay awake. Beneath her trembling fingers, the carpet seemed to writhe, its pattern shifting back and forth. She heard a ‘ding’ from the elevator. Jack’s footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder, but Jack’s momentum betrayed him as he crashed to the floor. Blood splattered in jagged streaks across the still shifting carpet. This was her moment. If not now, then when? Wendy got up, staggered, pain exploding in her side, and started running. Every step felt slow and heavy, as though she moved through quicksand. She imagined Jack rising behind her, unstoppable, coming closer by the second. She glanced back once, only once, before running headlong into the dark corridor.
written_by_MFA018.Reason: Excerpt 2 offers a nice and easy to understand sequence of events starting with the chase up the stairs and the threats from Jack who was in hot pursuit. The fear and terror that engulfed Wendy is clearly demonstrated accompanied by the reason for the fear. It is also easy to understand how and why the man  in a green ghoul mask is relevant to the story. In excerpt 1 it is impossible to know why he is relevant.

written_by_MFA018.Reason:
I really struggled to define which of the two was "better" as I feel like they are written in different styles. To briefly touch on Excerpt 1, I feel like it was written in a more literary fashion in which the author is trying to get you inside of the emotions and inner dialogue in Wendy's head. When done in a creative horror novel that someone is reading for entertainment, it can be effective as Stephen King himself demonstrated in most of his work (I was a major Stephen King fan in school). 

However, I selected Excerpt 2 as the ultimately "better" passage in terms of writing quality. I'll address why by touching on the three key points. In terms of clarity and coherence, I am able to understand and visualize what Wendy is experiencing both physically and mentally by the descriptive language the pushes the scene forward. When you look at both passages you get a better sense of physical movement and action in excerpt 2.Another argument for clarity lies in how there are less metaphors and ambiguous turns of phrase in excerpt 2. For instance, Jack describing crushing her bones like "garlic cloves" provokes a visceral image that most people can visualize and understand. In the other passage he uses an idiom "time for your medicine" to imply that he is going to cause her harm, which can be effective to a contextual English speaker but downright confusing to someone who is not as literate. The fact that except 2 uses simple and descriptive language like this makes it much more coherent for someone to dive into and read as it accommodates all reading proficiencies.

In terms of fluency, as mentioned previously, the passage in excerpt 2 feels like it follows a steady pace and is easy to visualize without wasting a lot of time on metaphor and emotion. You envision Wendy running up stairs, being chased by Jack, going up what feels like endless spiral stairs only to make it to the top where she immediately encounters the next problem and moves on. I think of fluency as your ability to pace out and follow the action of the story without being confused. While a reader like me might appreciate the descriptive and poetic language of excerpt 1, I feel the majority of readers are looking to see what happens in the story that captivates their attention.

The fluency and coherence and simplicity of the writing in excerpt 2 ultimately speak to the passages effectiveness. I know from context that this appears to be either from or a rewritten portion of Stephen King's the Shining. Given that a reader would go into a novel like this expecting it to be scary and tense, excerpt 2 sells this concept by sticking quickly to the action and simple description to move the plot along quickly. While King is capable of doing this, most readers will not be terrified by overly descriptive metaphorical writing. However, that's not to say excerpt 2 is only action. The arrival of the "man-or something similar to a man-" in excerpt 2 is the kind of ambiguous sudden horrific image that can stick in a readers mind and horrify them.

Her fingers dug into the carpet, her nails scraping the fibers, as the texture seemed to undulate beneath her touch. The elevator chimed in the distance, and her stomach turned as she realized he’d found another way up. Jack lunged forward, his momentum carrying him past her, and he hit the floor with a wet thud. Blood pooled beneath his face, staining the carpet in a grotesque bloom of crimson. Wendy blinked, the world tilting, as she willed herself to rise. The monster was down, but not out. Her escape depended on seconds, and the clock was still ticking.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: Wendy could barely breathe as she ran up the old, creaking staircase, Jack close behind. “I’m gonna cave your head in, Wendy!” he screamed gleefully up at her, swinging his roque mallet back and forth in the air. Blood oozed out of his grinning mouth and down his chin. He looked like a real maniac, some deranged and bloodthirsty maniac. That gave Wendy the push she needed to block out her pain and pick up her pace. As she reached the next floor and darted through a connected corridor, a door suddenly swung open. A man emerged. He wore a rubbery and ghoulish green mask that seemed to be part of a Halloween costume. “Sing, dance, come celebrate! The party’s just starting!” he shouted, voice booming like a thunderstorm, and pulled the string on a party popper. A crack like lightning. The startling party favor spit confetti into the hallway, and Wendy gasped. The man slammed the door, vanishing back into the room. For a moment Wendy felt ridiculous, as if this whole thing were staged and harmless, like a haunted house attraction at an amusement park. But her body’s brief relaxation brought back her pain, which burst through her side. She crumpled in agony to the floor, vision blurring, battling to keep herself conscious; the carpet moved under her fingers. She heard the elevator rumble again, and knew that Jack had caught up. “There she is! Smile for me!” He lunged at her, narrowly missing her head with his mallet. Too much momentum. He lost his balance and crashed to the floor beside her with a thud. Blood spraying out of his mouth and onto the carpet as his cheek hit the ground. His eyes stayed closed. Wendy’s heart skipped a beat and for a moment she thought it was over. Then Jack opened one eye, almost playfully, and reached for her. She crawled forward, pushing herself back up and into a gradual sprint but Jack’s heavy footfalls trailed not far behind.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: Wendy could barely breathe as she ran up the old, creaking staircase, Jack close behind. “I’m gonna cave your head in, Wendy!” he screamed gleefully up at her, swinging his roque mallet back and forth in the air. Blood oozed out of his grinning mouth and down his chin. He looked like a real maniac, some deranged and bloodthirsty maniac. That gave Wendy the push she needed to block out her pain and pick up her pace. As she reached the next floor and darted through a connected corridor, a door suddenly swung open. A man emerged. He wore a rubbery and ghoulish green mask that seemed to be part of a Halloween costume. “Sing, dance, come celebrate! The party’s just starting!” he shouted, voice booming like a thunderstorm, and pulled the string on a party popper. A crack like lightning. The startling party favor spit confetti into the hallway, and Wendy gasped. The man slammed the door, vanishing back into the room. For a moment Wendy felt ridiculous, as if this whole thing were staged and harmless, like a haunted house attraction at an amusement park. But her body’s brief relaxation brought back her pain, which burst through her side. She crumpled in agony to the floor, vision blurring, battling to keep herself conscious; the carpet moved under her fingers. She heard the elevator rumble again, and knew that Jack had caught up. “There she is! Smile for me!” He lunged at her, narrowly missing her head with his mallet. Too much momentum. He lost his balance and crashed to the floor beside her with a thud. Blood spraying out of his mouth and onto the carpet as his cheek hit the ground. His eyes stayed closed. Wendy’s heart skipped a beat and for a moment she thought it was over. Then Jack opened one eye, almost playfully, and reached for her. She crawled forward, pushing herself back up and into a gradual sprint but Jack’s heavy footfalls trailed not far behind.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath came in ragged gasps, the sharp pain in her side like a splintered knife twisting deeper with each step. Jack’s laughter echoed up the staircase, a sound that was both guttural and gleeful, like a hyena that had found its prey. His mallet thudded against the bannister, a syncopated rhythm to the rising panic in her chest. She clawed at the handrail, her legs burning, her mind screaming for her body to keep moving.The corridor at the top of the stairs stretched out like a warped funhouse hallway. Shadows wavered on the walls, flickering with the uneven glow of the overhead bulbs. Wendy’s vision blurred, the carpet beneath her feet seeming to ripple like water. She stumbled but didn’t fall, her hand brushing the wall for balance as she pushed forward. A door burst open on her left, and a man in a green ghoul mask leapt out, his arms wide in mock celebration. “Party time!” he bellowed, the sound shrill and manic, accompanied by the wheezy squeal of a party favor. Wendy recoiled, her scream caught in her throat, as the ghoul slammed the door shut behind him, the sound echoing like a judge’s gavel.Jack’s voice boomed behind her, slurring threats that mixed rage with twisted humor. “Here’s Johnny!” The mallet whooshed through the air, missing her by inches as she collapsed against the wall. Her fingers dug into the carpet, her nails scraping the fibers, as the texture seemed to undulate beneath her touch. The elevator chimed in the distance, and her stomach turned as she realized he’d found another way up. Jack lunged forward, his momentum carrying him past her, and he hit the floor with a wet thud. Blood pooled beneath his face, staining the carpet in a grotesque bloom of crimson. Wendy blinked, the world tilting, as she willed herself to rise. The monster was down, but not out. Her escape depended on seconds, and the clock was still ticking.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better quality writing than excerpt 1. It takes you through a real-time experience of terror. You feel the pursuit happening in real time. The descriptions of gore and horror are done with more imagery and more fluent language in excerpt 2. Contrast excerpt 1's scene here: "Blood spraying out of his mouth and onto the carpet as his cheek hit the ground" with excerpt 2's version of the same incident "Blood pooled beneath his face, staining the carpet in a grotesque bloom of crimson". Excerpt 2 is vivid and active. The blood is pooling and spilling out in a violent stain of dark red. Excerpt 1 describes this very upsetting and frightening scene with the same passion you might describe a skinned knee. Very low impact and it doesn't elicit the same fear and terror as excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I closed my eyes and thought about the nature of longing, how it shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel, becoming more precise in its form the more complete the void becomes. Sylvie had left in that way of hers, without sound or ceremony, as if she had simply dissolved into the thick afternoon air, and I found myself studying the treeline where the shadows gathered, imagining her watching me pretend not to notice the solitude she had left behind. There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.

written_by_MFA005.Reason: I am going to say excerpt one demonstrates better quality in writing. Coherently, I can understand that the narrator is reflecting on how lonely she is after Sylvie abandons her in the meadow. This is provocatively done with an image "I searched for Sylvie's hand besides mind, but I found she had slipped away silently". This is an example of "showing" the reader the idea naturally through scenic imagery rather than explicitly telling the reader that Sylvie left the clearing. Both excerpts are a little weak on the fluid and natural writing side, but excerpt 1 does give us a sense of the narrators reflectiveness over the events transpiring. I had to read both excerpts multiple times to understand the events, not sure if Sylvie was a long gone person or someone who just left in the moment the two characters got to the meadow. When trying to comprehend this event, excerpt 1 stood out to be as naturally making that more clear. This shows that the writer of that passage knows how to move the narrative along. Lastly, I will point at one example in both passages that demonstrates the effectiveness of excerpt 1: the symbolism of Sylvie being Lot's wife. Excerpt 2 simply states this metaphor directly "She would be like Lot's wife but not that in that she was barren and regretted what she had left behind." This is not effective as it hits the reader on the head with what the metaphor of Sylvie is. Excerpt 1 is more effective as it alludes to a woman who had turned to salt, which a careful reader would immediately call to mind the image of and understand the quality of the writing on a deeper level.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: It was the longing itself that seemed to summon the essence of what I desired, as if yearning were a prayer that the world, in its quiet way, conspired to answer. The sweetness of berries unpicked lingered in the air, more vibrant for being out of reach. Sylvie had vanished again, her silence as deliberate as a shadow retreating with the sun, and I knew not to call for her. It was better to let the absence settle, to imagine her slender frame paused just out of sight, watching from the line of trees, her face half-lit by the dappled sun. The woods held their breath, alive with the hum of insects and the rustle of unseen creatures, and I found myself wondering if she had gone into them to become something wilder, freer, more elemental than her mortal self. It was then I imagined a statue, a woman wrought from the alabaster of my mind, her form unyielding yet softened by an artist’s hand. Her hair, an eternal cascade of rare blossoms, reached toward the ground like a benediction. She would not be like Lot’s wife, turned back toward despair, but a figure of grace, fixed in forgiveness, her face turned forward into the eternal now.Around her feet would gather children, wild-eyed and untamed, the sort that flit through the forest like whispers of untold stories. They would marvel at her beauty, her quiet presence, her promise of solace, though her hands, stiff and unyielding, could never stroke their hair or lift them from their loneliness. And yet, the children would linger, imagining themselves known, loved, by the depths of her unseeing gaze. Perhaps Sylvie, wherever she was, could understand such a figure—one who existed between the realms of presence and absence, neither gone nor wholly there. The trees would hold her as their own, casting shadows that shifted like whispers against her alabaster skin. And I, rooted in my own solitude, could only wonder if longing itself was a form of creation, if absence was a kind of grace, and if Sylvie’s silence spoke a language deeper than words.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Christ almighty, here we are - trapped in this feverish documentation of a madman's journey, watching the words crawl across the page like speed-crazed insects searching for meaning in the neon wasteland between Hollywood and Vegas. The story reeks of desperate chemicals and the acrid stench of burning rubber on asphalt, all wrapped up in the frenzied quest for the Great American Convertible. My attorney, that chrome-domed harbinger of chaos, is barking into payphones at terrified salesmen while I hover near the bar of some godforsaken Polynesian tomb, mainlining Singapore Slings and wondering if we'll ever make it out of LA alive. The whole scene has the surgical precision of a hurricane - first the maniac phone calls, then the ugly business with the recording equipment, and somewhere in between, the grotesque spectacle of that poor bastard getting mowed down by a Stingray on Sunset. Jesus, what a place. What a time. The salesmen are wielding tire irons now, passing our gear through a crack in the door like they're feeding raw meat to a cage full of rabid wolverines. Can't blame them, really - not with what's happening out there in the streets. The whole country's gone belly-up with fear and loathing, and here we are, two professional journalists, supposedly documenting this circus of depravity. But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong. The evidence is everywhere: in the twisted metal on Sunset, in the paranoid eyes of the salesmen, in the heinous chemicals coursing through our bloodstreams like electric eels in a bathtub. And somehow we're supposed to make sense of it all, turn it into something resembling journalism. What a goddamn joke. But there's no going back now - we've bought the ticket, and by God, we're going to take the ride.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The attorney was on the phone, his voice a guttural rasp against the faux-Polynesian backdrop of the bar. "Red," he barked, "not pink. And make it snappy, the goddamn plane leaves in three hours."  I swiveled on the barstool, the vinyl squeaking in protest, and surveyed the wreckage of our preparations. Empty Mai Tai glasses stood like fallen soldiers, casualties in the war against sobriety. A crumpled napkin bore the cryptic message,"Convertible. Red. Not a goddamn boat."Outside, the Hollywood sun beat down with the malevolence of a loan shark. A pack of tourists shuffled past, their eyes glazed over with the vacant stare of the terminally sunburned. A low-slung Stingray roared by, leaving behind the faint scent of burnt rubber and the echo of a scream.  "Jesus," I muttered, "this town is a goddamn meat grinder."The attorney slammed the phone down, his face a mask of grim determination. "Got it," he snarled, "a red convertible. Picking it up in an hour."  He fixed me with a bloodshot stare. "Now, about that recording equipment..."We found the electronics store tucked away in a seedy strip mall, sandwiched between a bail bondsman and an adult bookstore. The salesmen eyed us with the suspicion of a pit bull eyeing a poodle. "We're closed," one growled, brandishing a tire iron."Bullshit," the attorney snarled back, "we just need some high-quality recording equipment. And we're in a hurry."  The door cracked open a few inches, revealing a glimpse of darkened aisles and the glint of chrome. A hand emerged, clutching a hefty price list. "Cash only," a voice rasped.An hour later, we emerged from the store, blinking against the harsh sunlight. The attorney clutched a bag crammed with microphones, recorders, and enough batteries to power a small city. I hefted a suitcase filled with enough "heinous chemicals" to fuel a weekend-long bender.We piled into the waiting convertible, the red paint gleaming like a fresh coat of blood. The attorney gunned the engine, and we roared off into the desert, leaving behind the madness of Hollywood and heading towards the even greater madness of Las Vegas.  The wind whipped through our hair, carrying with it the scent of freedom and the promise of adventure. This was the Gonzo life, and we were riding it full throttle, straight into the heart of the American Dream.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

"Now, about that recording equipment..."We found the electronics store tucked away in a seedy strip mall, sandwiched between a bail bondsman and an adult bookstore. The door cracked open a few inches, revealing a glimpse of darkened aisles and the glint of chrome. A hand emerged, clutching a hefty price list. "Cash only," a voice rasped.An hour later, we emerged from the store, blinking against the harsh sunlight. The attorney gunned the engine, and we roared off into the desert, leaving behind the madness of Hollywood and heading towards the even greater madness of Las Vegas.  The wind whipped through our hair, carrying with it the scent of freedom and the promise of adventure. This was the Gonzo life, and we were riding it full throttle, straight into the heart of the American Dream.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: I prefer excerpt 1 because overall I think that the story goes straight into the action without having to work on building the world up first. I like knowing the action first and seeing where the story was going what the plan was and how they planned to execute it. I wanted to keep reading and see what happens next.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The irony of Walter's transformation from eco-warrior to coal industry collaborator wasn't lost on the former neighbors in Ramsey Hill, though they nursed their disappointment with the kind of passive-aggressive Midwestern restraint that had always made Patty want to scream into her wine glass. In the early days, watching him pedal off to work on his secondhand Schwinn, his messenger bag stuffed with environmental impact reports and local-economy manifestos, the neighbors had seen him as a kind of secular saint, the sort of man who made them feel better about their own smaller gestures toward planetary salvation. Patty, meanwhile, had performed her own theatre of domestic virtue, pushing that double-wide stroller past crack houses and shuttered storefronts with the kind of aggressive cheer that suggested she was either oblivious to danger or actively courting it. The Victorian they'd bought for a song had been their shared project, their statement of faith in the possibility of redemption – not just of a house or a neighborhood, but of a whole way of life that was vanishing as surely as the ozone layer they worried about while listening to All Things Considered. Every stripped floorboard and replastered wall had seemed to say: See? This is how you do it. This is how you live righteously in a fallen world. But righteousness, it turned out, was a kind of intoxicant, and Walter had drunk deeper than most. The coal deal was just the logical endpoint of his conviction that he alone could save the world – a conviction that had grown more desperate and less discriminating as the world had shown itself increasingly resistant to being saved. The neighbors, sipping their own carefully sourced wine and tending their own carefully curated gardens, could afford to judge him now, secure in the knowledge that they, at least, had never tried quite so hard to be good.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In the quiet confines of Ramsey Hill, the news of Walter Berglund's troubles, as trumpeted by the unforgiving clarion of The New York Times, seemed to echo in a vacuum, its resonance muffled by the simple fact that Walter and Patty had moved to Washington, D.C., two years prior.  It was as if the man portrayed in the article - arrogant, ethically compromised - was a stranger, a doppelganger bearing little resemblance to the Walter they thought they knew.  The Walter they remembered was the lone cyclist, a beacon of environmental idealism in a sea of gas-guzzling SUVs, not someone enmeshed in the murky depths of coal industry dealings.But life, like memory, is a fickle thing, prone to distortions and revisions.  The Berglunds, in their Ramsey Hill days, were pioneers of a sort, young urban homesteaders staking their claim in a neighborhood that had seen better days.  Their Victorian house, a relic of a bygone era, was a testament to their tireless efforts, a monument to sweat equity built amidst the blight of boarded-up windows and rampant vandalism.Patty, a former college athlete, stood out in this gritty landscape, a figure of unflinching resilience pushing her stroller through streets littered with broken glass and the detritus of urban decay.  She was a woman who could change a diaper with one hand while wielding a spackle knife with the other, a woman who could soothe a crying child while simultaneously warding off the advances of an aggressive panhandler.Her days fell into a familiar rhythm: the comforting drone of public radio, the midday reward of a zinfandel, the constant juggling act of motherhood and home renovation.  She was a woman straddling two worlds, one foot planted in the world of middle-class aspirations, the other in the harsh reality of her surroundings. And yet, beneath this veneer of normalcy, there was a hint of vulnerability, a flicker of something unfulfilled.  The Berglunds, for all their outward success, were a study in contrasts, a living embodiment of the American Dream's inherent contradictions.  They were remarkable and yet flawed, their idealism tempered by the compromises and disappointments of life.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”

The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: In the quiet confines of Ramsey Hill, the news of Walter Berglund's troubles, as trumpeted by the unforgiving clarion of The New York Times, seemed to echo in a vacuum, its resonance muffled by the simple fact that Walter and Patty had moved to Washington, D.C., two years prior.  It was as if the man portrayed in the article - arrogant, ethically compromised - was a stranger, a doppelganger bearing little resemblance to the Walter they thought they knew.  The Walter they remembered was the lone cyclist, a beacon of environmental idealism in a sea of gas-guzzling SUVs, not someone enmeshed in the murky depths of coal industry dealings.But life, like memory, is a fickle thing, prone to distortions and revisions.  The Berglunds, in their Ramsey Hill days, were pioneers of a sort, young urban homesteaders staking their claim in a neighborhood that had seen better days.  Their Victorian house, a relic of a bygone era, was a testament to their tireless efforts, a monument to sweat equity built amidst the blight of boarded-up windows and rampant vandalism.Patty, a former college athlete, stood out in this gritty landscape, a figure of unflinching resilience pushing her stroller through streets littered with broken glass and the detritus of urban decay.  She was a woman who could change a diaper with one hand while wielding a spackle knife with the other, a woman who could soothe a crying child while simultaneously warding off the advances of an aggressive panhandler.Her days fell into a familiar rhythm: the comforting drone of public radio, the midday reward of a zinfandel, the constant juggling act of motherhood and home renovation.  She was a woman straddling two worlds, one foot planted in the world of middle-class aspirations, the other in the harsh reality of her surroundings. And yet, beneath this veneer of normalcy, there was a hint of vulnerability, a flicker of something unfulfilled.  The Berglunds, for all their outward success, were a study in contrasts, a living embodiment of the American Dream's inherent contradictions.  They were remarkable and yet flawed, their idealism tempered by the compromises and disappointments of life.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: In the quiet confines of Ramsey Hill, the news of Walter Berglund's troubles, as trumpeted by the unforgiving clarion of The New York Times, seemed to echo in a vacuum, its resonance muffled by the simple fact that Walter and Patty had moved to Washington, D.C., two years prior.  It was as if the man portrayed in the article - arrogant, ethically compromised - was a stranger, a doppelganger bearing little resemblance to the Walter they thought they knew.  The Walter they remembered was the lone cyclist, a beacon of environmental idealism in a sea of gas-guzzling SUVs, not someone enmeshed in the murky depths of coal industry dealings.But life, like memory, is a fickle thing, prone to distortions and revisions.  The Berglunds, in their Ramsey Hill days, were pioneers of a sort, young urban homesteaders staking their claim in a neighborhood that had seen better days.  Their Victorian house, a relic of a bygone era, was a testament to their tireless efforts, a monument to sweat equity built amidst the blight of boarded-up windows and rampant vandalism.Patty, a former college athlete, stood out in this gritty landscape, a figure of unflinching resilience pushing her stroller through streets littered with broken glass and the detritus of urban decay.  She was a woman who could change a diaper with one hand while wielding a spackle knife with the other, a woman who could soothe a crying child while simultaneously warding off the advances of an aggressive panhandler.Her days fell into a familiar rhythm: the comforting drone of public radio, the midday reward of a zinfandel, the constant juggling act of motherhood and home renovation.  She was a woman straddling two worlds, one foot planted in the world of middle-class aspirations, the other in the harsh reality of her surroundings. And yet, beneath this veneer of normalcy, there was a hint of vulnerability, a flicker of something unfulfilled.  The Berglunds, for all their outward success, were a study in contrasts, a living embodiment of the American Dream's inherent contradictions.  They were remarkable and yet flawed, their idealism tempered by the compromises and disappointments of life.
