written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 2 is easier to understand and you can picture the characters in your mind as you read it. The first excerpt is too abstract and although descriptive, it is hard to follow along. Excerpt 2 flows more naturally like a book or movie and you can imagine what the people are doing.

The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We looked around the hotel room when we opened the door. To be away together! Catherine’s arm looped around my shoulders with mine around her waist. She’d been clearer to me than myself, because I didn’t spend all day studying myself the way I spent all day studying her. My investigation was not complete. We made drinks and sat in the corner chairs. It didn’t matter much that we hadn’t been in the room before. A sense of being at home, of familiarity, accompanied me with Catherine wherever we went together. Rain came down outside in long slants and we listened to the sound in between our conversations and during our sips of drink. The glasses emptied and we filled them up. We could sit in silence, alone with our thoughts but connected somehow. There was the pleasure of watching another think without fear of being caught. She might have even had the expectation of me watching her think. With others long moments of silence had an itchy quality. With friends and lovers I had clawed back into conversation when it faltered or ended naturally. This time as we lay in bed gazing around at the room my mind wandered to those distant relationships and those people who hadn’t met someone like Catherine. Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited. I reached out and touched her skin and watched my finger trace a white line down her shoulder. A melancholy settled over me. The nature of the world when taken without this comfort breaks everyone and kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. Perhaps those who suffer this fate can persevere for a time or recover from its cruelty in short bursts. Still, suffer they will. When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I lay in the hotel bed with Catherine, listening to the rain beat against the windows, and I felt good. Really good. The sheets were cool and smooth, and Catherine's breathing was soft and even beside me, and for the first time in a long while I wasn't alone. Not the way you can be alone in a crowded café or alone in someone else's bed, but really not alone. We didn't need to talk. That was the fine thing about Catherine. You could be quiet with her and it felt right. The rain kept coming down outside and the street lamps made yellow pools on the wet pavement below, and I watched them and felt Catherine's warmth against me, solid and real. I had been with other women before, plenty of them, but it was always like being alone, even when you were holding them. With Catherine it was different. She knew about being alone too, and maybe that's why we could be alone together without it hurting. The world breaks everyone sooner or later, that's what I'd learned. It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. But Catherine and I, we were already broken when we found each other, so maybe that's why we fit. We didn't need to pretend. The rain was coming down harder now, drumming against the roof, and Catherine stirred beside me but didn't wake. I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true. But for now we had this - the rain outside and the warm bed and the knowledge that we weren't alone. Sometimes that's all you get in this world, these small moments of peace before the breaking starts again. But maybe if you're lucky, you find someone who knows how to pick up the pieces with you. Catherine knew about pieces. She knew about breaking. And here in this room, with the rain coming down, we had put our broken pieces together and made something whole.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The hotel balcony looked out through the rain down to the riviera. The houses outside were gray. In the dark we listened to the rain on the roof, and Catherine turned to me to say nothing, and we lay like that for a while. The slope of her shoulder was like a mountain. It could have always been there like a mountain in the distance, and I could have not known I'd memorized it. Then she spoke. "Do you need me tomorrow?""Shush. Shush," I said. I didn't like that I had to say it. It was that knowledge of what not to say that filled more in me than any words could. She turned away. The rain hit thick on the balcony tiles. The sheets felt soft. I wanted her to focus on that. The sheets, the small room, the wind blowing the rain sideways. We didn't burn the lights and let the moon through the thin curtain show. In similar rooms and nights like these, I had felt the worst of them alone. What I didn't know I needed was that same stifled quiet, the same rain, the same room. Perhaps I expected less of me to fill it all. I felt at home when I felt her most and heard her least. With the crowded taverns, I'd go and sit between stone shoulders and feel no need of my being there. What made her mine was what she never asked of me."Maybe tomorrow," I said. She said nothing. The rain whipped on. Soon, the streets outside would be muddy and thick. The mud would cake our shoes. The ground at its meanest like that. It takes us at its softest. The ground breaks everyone it breaks itself for. All men, the very good and the very gentle and the very brave, all go quiet in the ground. It clings and cakes to you. Yet you can pull. Yet you can crawl and drag onto more mud, more breaking, more ground that will eventually take you."Maybe tomorrow you come with me," I still said to the rain.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The rain was a constant companion that night, its soft patter against the window a soothing melody. I lay in bed, the sheets a cool caress against my skin, and felt a warmth bloom within me. It was a warmth that had nothing to do with the fire crackling in the hearth, but rather with the presence beside me. Catherine. My Catherine. With her there, I felt a sense of belonging, a feeling of completeness that I had never experienced before.We had always possessed this uncanny ability, Catherine and I, to be utterly alone, yet entirely together.  In the past, I had often found myself adrift in a sea of faces, surrounded by people, yet feeling utterly isolated.  But with Catherine, it was as if we created our own world, a world where words were unnecessary, where our thoughts flowed together like two streams merging into one.  We could sit in silence, and yet I felt a connection deeper than any I had ever known.Tonight, however, there was a different kind of silence between us, a silence tinged with a sadness that I couldn't quite shake off.  The world, I reflected, was a brutal and unforgiving place.  It was a place that left its mark on everyone, breaking the strongest of hearts and extinguishing the brightest of spirits.  It killed the very good, the very gentle, and the very brave, leaving the rest of us to stumble on, wounded and weary.And yet, there was a strange beauty in this brokenness, a resilience that emerged from the ashes of suffering.  Those who survived, those who had been forged in the fires of adversity, they possessed a strength that could not be denied.  They had been broken, yes, but they had also been tempered, their spirits honed by the world's harshness.I glanced at Catherine, her face serene in sleep, and felt a wave of love wash over me. She was my sanctuary, my refuge, the one person who could make me feel whole.  And in that moment, I knew that even in the face of the world's cruelty, our love would be our salvation.

While excerpt 2 is clear it feels more generic.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: The rain came hard against the window, steady and thin, running down in lines like wire. The room was warm, the sheets smooth beneath my hand. There was time for everything now, and it felt like all the time in the world.She stirred but did not wake. I watched her for a while. I had been alone before. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The club's mahogany-paneled dining room felt both intimate and imposing, much like the billionaire himself who sat across from me in his unexpectedly casual attire - a contradiction that seemed to epitomize the entire encounter. He spoke of his software project with the same blithe enthusiasm one might discuss a hobby, though its purpose - to predict employee betrayal - carried an unmistakable darkness beneath its technological sheen. I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better because the story is more connected, and more thoughtful especially from the setting to the billionaire’s character, and the language feels elegant and poetic for example when the narrator says they felt like “a surface upon which his life story was being projected"Everything resonates with each other and comes back to the software the billonaire mentioned.

I was late, carrying my heavy suitcase and sweating, but the billionaire wore casual clothes and seemed unbothered by my lateness, launching into an explanation of his software project for predicting employee betrayal. The literary journal had not come up when the waitress brought bread to us, nor when she brought a range of appetizers. I realized the billionaire had ordered for us both. He insisted then on paying for a taxi to the airport, a generosity I would not decline given the rush of my morning. As we ate, he unfurled his life story. ‘It’s all what you’d expect,’ he said. ‘Rags-to-riches, you know—to be rich and unbothered, that’s the real achievement. To feel calm,’ he told me. ‘That’s what it allows.’ I wondered if he thought of the literary magazine as an entry point into writing. Everyone wants to write, I’ve noticed; everyone imagines themselves a writer, even if they have never put pen to paper. The billionaire had funded a good many ambitious ventures. A floating wind farm with worker houses, and something about a scheme to eliminate lawyers for managing personal matters. The waitress brought small plates, caviar and shaved truffle and mint suspended artfully over a scallop. The billionaire played drums in a rock band to relax. He was expecting his eleventh child, a number of children he knew and hoped that I would balk at, and explained that four of his children were adopted Guatemalan quadruplets. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: The coherence of excerpt 2 impressed me more, as I believe the story flows a lot better. It seemed to be in a more chronological order starting simply with 'I was invited to lunch by a billionaire' and carrying on into why they were there, where they were and what was happening in a descriptive yet fluent way. It is effective as it puts the story across whilst still allowing the reader to imagine the setting of an opulent London Club with 'gilded light fixtures and dark accents'. Excerpt 1 tries to do this but is too descriptive at the cost of a coherent story line. For example, it repeats too many times about he 'spoke of his ventures'.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The billionaire, in his casual attire, was an unexpected sight in the opulent setting of the London club, a stark contrast to the tailored suits and formal dresses that adorned the other patrons.  He spoke first of a software project, a tool designed to predict employee betrayal, a concept that seemed both futuristic and unsettlingly Orwellian.The purpose of our meeting, however, was to discuss a literary magazine he was keen to establish, a venture that seemed oddly out of place with his technological pursuits. As the conversation meandered, he insisted on paying for a taxi to the airport, a practical gesture considering my lateness and the cumbersome suitcase I was lugging. Over the course of the meal, he shared his life story, a narrative that began humbly but had culminated in the affluent, relaxed figure before me.  I couldn't help but speculate that the magazine was perhaps another avenue for him to conquer, another domain to enter as he had done with so many others through the sheer force of his wealth. He recounted his rags-to-riches journey, his various ambitious ventures - a floating wind farm complete with worker housing, a scheme to eliminate lawyers from personal matters.  He spoke of these ventures with a childlike enthusiasm, his eyes gleaming with the thrill of innovation and the satisfaction of having brought his ideas to fruition.  He even mentioned playing drums in a rock band for leisure and the anticipation of his eleventh child, including adopted Guatemalan quadruplets. written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The club's interior held that particular London stillness, a cultivated hush that seemed to absorb and neutralize the city's chaos beyond its walls. The billionaire sat opposite me in jeans and a t-shirt, his casualness a subtle assertion of power in this formal setting, as though the rules that governed others were merely suggestions to him. He spoke rapidly about his software project - designed to predict employee betrayal - with the enthusiastic self-absorption of someone unused to interruption. I found myself studying the way he moved his hands, which were unexpectedly delicate, as he described algorithms that could detect disloyalty in email patterns. The waitresses appeared and disappeared like synchronized dancers, bearing plates of increasingly elaborate food that he barely seemed to notice. When he mentioned the literary magazine he wanted to start, I recognized in his tone that particular quality of the very wealthy - the assumption that anything could be acquired or created through the application of sufficient capital. His life story emerged in fragments between courses: the humble beginnings, the Guatemalan quadruplets, the floating wind farm with its worker housing, each achievement recounted with a child's pride in showing off their toys. I noticed how he used the word "just" before describing extraordinary accomplishments - "I just bought an island," "I just started a rock band" - as though trying to diminish their significance while simultaneously drawing attention to them. The scattered nature of his focus felt familiar to me, reminiscent of the way wealth itself tends to fragment experience into consumable pieces. When he mentioned my upcoming trip to Athens - something I hadn't told him about - I felt a curious shift in the air between us, as though the careful performance of our lunch had momentarily slipped to reveal something else beneath. But he was already moving on to another topic, and I found myself wondering if I had imagined it, the way one sometimes imagines connections between unrelated events in an attempt to create meaning from randomness. The taxi he insisted on paying for waited outside like a full stop at the end of a run-on sentence.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The billionaire had invited me to lunch with him at a London club. When I arrived, I was surprised by how casually he dressed, in jeans and a white button-down. He was generous: on account of my enormous suitcase, he offered to call me a taxi to the airport when it was time to leave. He told me he was working on a software project that could predict an employee's capacity to betray their company. I didn't know why we were talking about this—we were meeting under the pretense of discussing a literary magazine that the billionaire was interested in starting—but I sat there and did my best to listen. He wanted to tell me many things, his whole life story. He had grown up poor, he said, but that hadn't lasted long, and now he had a floating windfarm that doubled as worker housing, and an idea for a scheme to keep lawyers out of people's personal business. He told me about the rock band he played drums in, and that he was expecting his eleventh child soon. This was in addition to the four Guatemalan quadruplets he had already adopted. It felt like too many children to me. I wondered if perhaps he thought that by creating this magazine, he might also fashion himself as a writer capable of being published in it. The idea seemed a stretch to me, but perhaps the billionaire was used to spanning such extreme logical leaps. The leap from man to billionaire was certainly larger than billionaire to writer. I was struggling to follow my own line of thinking. The waitress kept appearing, bringing brightly colored drinks and dishes that alternated between tasting too rich and too pungent. It had the opposite effect on the billionaire. Amidst the bright colors and flavors, the billionaire's face shone like a young boy who had been suddenly surrounded by mountains of his favorite sweets. When the food and drink had finally been swept away and the bill paid, he put me and my heavy suitcase in the taxi. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, which was a surprise. I hadn't recalled ever mentioning my destination.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Excerpt 2 is absolutely more coherent. It delivers observations, and then theories or opinions about those observations (e.g., he said he was going to start a magazine-- maybe so he could get published in it? or he said he had a ton of kids-- I thought it was too many). Excerpt 1 makes the same statements, but leaves them unaddressed and, frankly, without context (the Guatemalan quadruplets are mentioned without clarity-- was this an adoption, or a sexual rendezvous?). Too much is left to be contrived by the reader, and because of this, the goals of the writing are lost. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, neatly portrays the relationship between the skeptical author and the flashy billionaire.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.

Excerpt 1 is less descriptive, includes run on sentences, and has less fluency which takes away from its impact. Excerpt 2 achieves its goals through high quality writing, fluidity, and great detail.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt two has a clear flow of ideas and that makes the message easily comprehended. Excerpt 1 mixes ideas between sickness and forced treaties and it's difficult to find the connection. Excerpt 2 gives a clear sequence of events and how they unfolded starting with the sickness, followed by malicious treaties and consumption which sounds like the last nail in the coffin for the community.

Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Reason:
Excerpt 1 sounds like a diss track or angry stomp poetry.  Maybe even an angry Facebook post from 2012.  It is effective in its raw emotion, but it is not exactly fluent or coherent.

Excerpt 2 reads as if someone put effort into writing what Excerpt 1 literarily meant.  There is a clear story without need for inference or reading between the lines.

Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 feels like a more natural usage of writing. There are grammatical errors but they feel in service to the character. Excerpt 2 has unnatural tendencies like capitalizing a word in the middle of a sentence ('Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go'), also examples of using dialogue without quotation.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: She was the one who said it, mi amor. "If you cheat on me, it's over."  And there it was, laid bare in her inbox: six years, fifty women, a betrayal that stretched back to the very beginning.  Your bad-ass salcedense fiancée, the one whose father you'd helped bury, whose law school dreams you'd supported, whose hand you'd held through the darkest nights, now stared at you with an emptiness that mirrored the hollow in your own chest.She didn't leave right away.  Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? Because you’re some sort of idiot hijo de cuero, but you knew that about yourself long before she found the emails. Fifty women jammed into six years–it’s almost impressive, when you think about it. Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: The story is clear in excerpt 1. It tells of how a man broke his fiancee's trust. Having 50 women in six years was horrible.He has tried to win her back but all to no avail. He travelled with her to the Dominican republic,Mexico and all the way to New Zealand just to passify her but the the trust was broken it could not be fixed

Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: She was the one who said it, mi amor. "If you cheat on me, it's over."  And there it was, laid bare in her inbox: six years, fifty women, a betrayal that stretched back to the very beginning.  Your bad-ass salcedense fiancée, the one whose father you'd helped bury, whose law school dreams you'd supported, whose hand you'd held through the darkest nights, now stared at you with an emptiness that mirrored the hollow in your own chest.She didn't leave right away.  Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: I really didn't understand much of what was going on in excerpt 1. It was very difficult to understand and make sense of. Excerpt 2 was a lot more descriptive and natural in the writing style and more effective in giving the reader details they needed to understand what was happening in the scenario

written_by_MFA028.Excerpt1: You come home. It’s hot--dead hot, like a puta in church. She’s home, and rat-fucking pissed, but that’s what you liked about her, isn’t it? Bad-ass salcedense, short hair, ass is the stuff of rumors. Throw a brick at a homeboy for looking at her funny. And this salcedense had to throw a couple bricks in her day. She walks by herself and you watch her. Well, you try not to. You walk up and say baby, baby, grab her ass, make a kiss like you mean it. But she’s cooked. She’s fried. She wants nothing to do with your black ass. What I’m sayin is negro, you’ve fucked up bad. On the way to the hotel, you see this couple, right? H-O-N-E-Y-M-O-O-N. Eyes like the ocean, can’t keep off each other. Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae. Like this is what it’s supposed to be. I don’t gotta tell you how that makes you feel. When you get back, she starts crying. Making fists, the whole thing. She says you’re not no fucking man. Her daddy warned her about you. But he’s fuckin dead.
written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.
written_by_MFA028.Reason: Oh man, Excerpt 2 is so good! Excerpt 1 is again pretty incoherent-- it takes the reader some work to piece together what is happening, and it's very "flow of thought." But Excerpt 2 tells the entire story, and the sentence "habit is its own kind of handcuff" is incredible for really driving home why the partner may have stayed. Honestly, Excerpt 2 is fluid and emotional and just really well-written.

But she found out, and it’s bad. Fifty women bad, and for six years. Plus you knew. Of course you fucking knew. She told you, you chancla-headed fuck, you slip once and she’s out. Well, cue the platano peel, because homie, you slipped. Fifty fucking girls. Once a year that’s half a siglo. She’s pissed, but it’s weird. Actually, you find out it’s chill. At least for a few months. Steady as it goes. Knew her too long, it turns out, through the job search, the bar, her father’s entierro. Can’t let go of a good thing. Even when she knows it’s bad. You kick off like that’ll help and hit the DR, CDM, fucking New Zealand. In NZ, fifty miles from Baggins Way, she says she dreamed this beach. Says it was in The Piano. She walks by herself and you watch her. Well, you try not to. You walk up and say baby, baby, grab her ass, make a kiss like you mean it. But she’s cooked. She’s fried. She wants nothing to do with your black ass. What I’m sayin is negro, you’ve fucked up bad. On the way to the hotel, you see this couple, right? H-O-N-E-Y-M-O-O-N. Eyes like the ocean, can’t keep off each other. Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae. Like this is what it’s supposed to be. I don’t gotta tell you how that makes you feel. When you get back, she starts crying. Making fists, the whole thing. She says you’re not no fucking man. Her daddy warned her about you. But he’s fuckin dead.
written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.
written_by_MFA028.Reason: 2 is much clearer to read and understand, making it more effective. 1 has a very strong narrative voice, but this takes away from coherence and fluency, making it quite confusing to read and understand. 2 is more consistent and clearly written, is smooth and structured and doesn't lose efficacy by having a less clear narrative voice.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

I found the first excerpt more engaging and the dialogue a bit more interesting overall.

As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "It's amazing, how the same things that happen between a man and a woman can be so different simply because of their race." The table, a mix of faces, both familiar and new, leaned in, intrigued. "But here, suddenly, I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm a Black woman dating a white man." She let out a small, humorless laugh. "It's like this whole other layer gets added, this… awareness, this constant hum in the background that you can't quite ignore." "But things are so much better now, no?" The Frenchwoman, her accent a delicate lilt, tilted her head. "You couldn't even… you know…" she trailed off, gesturing vaguely. "Marry each other?" She finished for her, feeling the familiar sting. "Yes, we've 'progressed.' Now we can be together, but we still have to tiptoe around all the unspoken things." She took another sip, the wine warming her throat, loosening her tongue. "Like, I can't get too angry, can't disagree too strongly, because then I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm the angry Black woman." "Oh, but that's…" the poet, his brow furrowed, shifted uncomfortably. "I mean, surely, it's not…" "Food's getting cold, don't you think?" Blaine, ever the diplomat, interjected smoothly. But she was on a roll, the words tumbling out, fueled by the wine and years of unspoken frustrations. "And it's not just him, it's everyone. This constant… need to remind me how far we've come. She met Blaine's eyes across the table, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, I want to… scream, to break free from this invisible script that everyone seems to have for me." A heavy silence settled over the table. She knew she was oversharing, knew she'd regret this in the morning. But tonight, the wine had given her a voice, a raw, unfiltered voice. "Like with Curt, for example…" she began, feeling a new wave of memories, a new wave of honesty, washing over her.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: P2 was my preferred excerpt. It felt more immediate from the first sentence - as readers we feel more closely connected to Ifemelu as we read that the wine pooled against her lips rather than she just sips it, somehow - we identify with her much strongly from the first, the writing feels more personal as we see the other guests very much through her eyes. The analogies felt more effective also - e.g. the weather reference

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.

She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad.
