written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

You need to use prose to elicit emotion from your reader, and phrases like "every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat" is way more effective than "laborers who built the White House!" The goal in Excerpt 1 is clear, and the entirety of the excerpt help to support that goal.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: The first passage is made up of a raw, conversational tone that makes the speaker’s emotion and concerns feel striking and almost personal. It contains plain language such as “too much blood,” and “grandest delusion” that portrays an actual lived experience rather than metaphor-laden abstraction. The tone is simple and accessible, allowing readers to join the author on their journey, whereas the second excerpt attempts to elevate itself via vivid imagery and symbolism through the use of grandeur language and  metaphor, which I believe heavily dilute the core message of the passage

White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Although there are a couple of strange phrases in excerpt 2, for example "a sanctuary where wouldn't follow" the excerpt flows more effectively.  It draws you in and keeps moving forward.   The flow is better potentially as it switches case less often and is more about "we" in the 2nd excerpt than in the first excerpt. It also feels like the sentences are shorter and more punchy.

The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Reason:
Excerpt 2 is the superior narrative.  The first one is disjointed.  Tenses get confused and some sentences are not grammatically correct.
This sentence fragment is a bit jarring:  

"a sanctuary where wouldn't follow?"

Excerpt 2's writing flows and the imagery makes sense and the topic of Valentine Farm is fleshed out.  It is much clearer to read and understand.

This sentence displays the superiority of one writing sample over the other: 

"All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different." is from Excerpt 2.

This is the same concept, a much wordier example from Excerpt 1:

"Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power,"

While this is not a bad passage, the succinct version works better and still gets the point across in Excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Both are good, to be honest, but if I had to choose, Excerpt 1 excelled slightly. It reads more poetic as opposed to the first-person narration-like style in Excerpt 2, so because of its poetic tone, it has a more effective outcome when reading it, almost like a tale of thought-provoking effects, which I quite prefer this writing style. I know it's not a part of the study specifically, but with Excerpt 2, the writing style is more confrontational, which can also be effective in itself, but taking into account how well the ideas flowed together, Excerpt 1 demonstrated that better

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo, the small fishing village near Busan where they had lived all their lives. Their eldest son Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, had survived while his two younger brothers had not. The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature. His parents had learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed – whether it was their son's conditions or the failures of their aristocratic rulers. When the rent increased again, they simply moved their own bedroom into the garden to make space for more lodgers, converting their former sleeping quarters into another room to let. Their kitchen now occupied a corner of the vegetable garden, the warm cooking smoke rising past clay roof tiles toward the evening sky. Some mornings, while preparing the lodgers' breakfast, the fisherman's wife would pause to watch the boats heading out to sea, their white sails bright against the gray dawn. She never envied the landlord's mansion in Busan with its Western furnishings and grand gates. Their modest wooden house with its sliding paper doors held everything they needed – space enough for lodgers whose rent helped them survive, a garden that provided vegetables for their soup, and most importantly, their son Hoonie, whose quiet strength and kind heart made their lives worth living. The other villagers often remarked on the family's fortitude, though the fisherman and his wife saw nothing remarkable in their way of life. To them, each day was simply another opportunity to work, to care for their son, and to maintain their dignity in a world that increasingly seemed to value only wealth and status. In Korea, as in most places, survival meant adapting to change without losing oneself, and this family had mastered that delicate balance through years of practiced resilience.
written_by_MFA029.Reason:
I like and prefer how quickly the scenery is established in the first few line. " In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo". 

A time period is given alongside a historical event to accompany that date. The fisherman and his wife are described as aging and non-confrontational. It is easier to imagine them as this given the culture and aftermath of conflict they have both likely experienced, whether directly or indirectly. 

It sets up the image of the family as selfless and hardworking so when I read further about their local deeds it simply reinforces my initial thoughts about them. The use of words like "Resilience", "Strength", "quiet" and "heart" to me highlight learned behaviours through very tough and stressful experiences which were required in a collective effort to survive.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The fisherman and his wife had lived in Yeongdo, a small village by the sea, for all their sixty years. Their lives, much like the ceaseless rhythm of the tides, were marked by an almost poetic blend of hardship and quiet resilience. The fisherman, his face etched with the map of a life spent battling the whims of the sea, had always been a man of few words, his weathered hands speaking volumes of his tireless labor. His wife had always been the anchor of their family, her hands calloused yet gentle, her spirit unyielding in the face of adversity. Over the years, they had welcomed three sons into the world, but only the eldest, Hoonie, had survived, a testament to the precarious nature of life in their humble village. Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, had always been a quiet observer, his physical limitations belying a keen mind and a gentle spirit. Hoonie, unfazed by their judgments, remained diligent and kind, his actions speaking louder than his words. In 1910, the year Japan annexed Korea, a tremor of political change rippled through their small world. Yet, the fisherman and his wife, their daily struggles, refused to dwell on the failures of their aristocratic rulers. Their concerns were more immediate, more tangible: the rising rent, the dwindling catch, the ever-present need to make ends meet. To supplement their meager income, they decided to take in lodgers, their small home expanding to accommodate strangers. They moved out of their own bedroom, their personal space sacrificed for the sake of their family's survival. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden, exposed to the elements, their meals prepared under the watchful gaze of the sky. Their home, a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof, stood in stark contrast to the opulent mansion of their landlord in Busan, a silent testament to the vast chasm that separated their worlds. Yet, within those humble walls, the fisherman and his wife had built a life, a testament to their enduring spirit, their unwavering love for their family.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: "Can he speak?" one of the lodgers asked, turning away from Hoonie and looking at his mother. Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. When Japan annexed Korea in 1910, their lives changed dramatically, but Hoonie's parents refused to dwell on the shortcomings of the aristocrats who ruled over them. Instead, they remained focused on their immediate concerns, kept their heads low, and provided for one another as best they could. Hoonie stood and bowed toward the lodger, who returned a subtle look of pity, then avoided eye contact altogether. He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt two has a much better sentence structure and flow. It also feels easier to read and understand than excerpt 1. I think in part this is from the use of passive voice in excerpt 1. Excerpt 2 feels much more engaging and inviting almost, as if you are a part of the story. There is a bit more active voice in excerpt two and you feel more engaged in excerpt 2.

Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. When Japan annexed Korea in 1910, their lives changed dramatically, but Hoonie's parents refused to dwell on the shortcomings of the aristocrats who ruled over them. Instead, they remained focused on their immediate concerns, kept their heads low, and provided for one another as best they could. Hoonie stood and bowed toward the lodger, who returned a subtle look of pity, then avoided eye contact altogether. He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The fisherman and his wife had lived in Yeongdo, a small village by the sea, for all their sixty years. Their lives, much like the ceaseless rhythm of the tides, were marked by an almost poetic blend of hardship and quiet resilience. The fisherman, his face etched with the map of a life spent battling the whims of the sea, had always been a man of few words, his weathered hands speaking volumes of his tireless labor. His wife had always been the anchor of their family, her hands calloused yet gentle, her spirit unyielding in the face of adversity. Over the years, they had welcomed three sons into the world, but only the eldest, Hoonie, had survived, a testament to the precarious nature of life in their humble village. Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, had always been a quiet observer, his physical limitations belying a keen mind and a gentle spirit. Hoonie, unfazed by their judgments, remained diligent and kind, his actions speaking louder than his words. In 1910, the year Japan annexed Korea, a tremor of political change rippled through their small world. Yet, the fisherman and his wife, their daily struggles, refused to dwell on the failures of their aristocratic rulers. Their concerns were more immediate, more tangible: the rising rent, the dwindling catch, the ever-present need to make ends meet. To supplement their meager income, they decided to take in lodgers, their small home expanding to accommodate strangers. They moved out of their own bedroom, their personal space sacrificed for the sake of their family's survival. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden, exposed to the elements, their meals prepared under the watchful gaze of the sky. Their home, a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof, stood in stark contrast to the opulent mansion of their landlord in Busan, a silent testament to the vast chasm that separated their worlds. Yet, within those humble walls, the fisherman and his wife had built a life, a testament to their enduring spirit, their unwavering love for their family.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: Excerpt two is better because it read more so like a story. There is a clear start, middle, and end which the first excerpt was lacking. Excerpt one also felt more rushed, while excerpt two had more flow. Excerpt one also felt like one big run-on sentence, while excerpt two was more complete.

There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: I think paragraph 2 is stronger as it uses more description, for example "like golden scales", which is quite imaginative. It also engages the reader by creating more visualisation. It feels more like a novel, the sentences flow well. The sentences in paragraph 1 can be harder to follow, and also lack the level of description paragraph 2 has.
